item.title: 5 Questions for Mehdi Paryavi
item.description: 5 Questions for Mehdi Paryavi
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from Hassan Ali Kanu

Mehdi Paryavi | International Data Center Authority handout.

Mehdi Paryavi is the chairman and CEO of the International Data Center Authority, a digital economy think tank that focuses on cloud computing, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. Under Paryavi’s leadership, IDCA has established international technical standards for data centers. He’s also worked with NASA, the governments of Oman and Ghana, and Google to build digital infrastructure. Paryavi recently testified before the United Nations on the natural resource implications of AI, and IDCA has since entered a multi-year partnership with the UN to accelerate the development of sustainable technology. He talks to us about prospective subscription services for intelligence, and the risk of data centers becoming obsolete. 

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Subscriptions. Everything is becoming a utility that you subscribe to. Just like you receive internet service, energy and gas to your home, you will potentially receive intelligence and access to the world through subscriptions. Subscriptions are something that have not really been discussed, but it is the underlying element that is driving the future of much of what you see around you — because that's the business model, and the definition of life as we know it in the coming years.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

The technology that's both underhyped and overhyped is AI. AI is underhyped because nobody has a grasp of the extent to which it can impact your life: How it can both improve progress and at the same time degrade your critical thinking, your mental conditioning.

But also, it’s overhyped because the claim is that it will basically do everything. There is a lot of human intervention. We are the ones as human beings who are making AI as capable as it is. We [facilitate] AI learning, so that in the future we can have AI inference. We are the ones as a human population educating AI, providing it the metadata, taking it through trial and error, and the maturity process.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

The most important thing that governments need to do is to understand technology. They don't know the implications of technology and AI for households, for social bonds, for economic prosperity. They don't understand the infrastructure requirements to uplift communities to be able to cater to AI needs. We need to build computing capabilities and capacities, otherwise we will miss the race. How do you build that without hurting communities, without hurting the environment? Where is the balance?

We need to make sure [politicians] have the credentials, experience and expertise to drive not only the cities and the counties and the states, but also entire countries into the new era. AI cannot run in silos. It needs energy, resources, manpower, submarine cable connectivity. There are so many interdependencies. It is not as simple as: “Let me build my data centers.”

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Civilizations: Ten Thousand Years of Ancient History by Jane McIntosh and Clint Twist. The future is nothing but a reflection of the past. When you read the history of humanity, you see the ups and downs of empires and civilizations. Arrogance is the number one enemy to any empire. AI can change the way you and I search for things or read things, but it cannot change the human experience. You can follow the trends of history, and the trends say one thing: If you are hungry, passionate, innovative, if you make the right alliances, you will lead the future.

If the technology of the future 5,000 years ago was fire, you could rule if you made the best of fire. If today it is AI, the same concept applies. You still need to be humble and collaborate with the rest of the world, and you still need to be hungry. And you must make sure that you take your population and your people with you.

What has surprised you the most this year?

The biggest surprise was a few months ago when [Nvidia CEO] Jensen Huang said [the company] will sell a trillion dollars of chips. Not many people understand what that means. To sell chips, you need to build data centers. To build data centers, you need energy and a workforce. Both of them do not exist today. We don't have enough workforce to run data centers and the hundreds of gigawatts of energy that is required.

The second thing is … if I build a $10 billion data center around this chip, in one year the chip is going to be revolutionized to a point that this data center looks obsolete. I have killed and depreciated that asset. That creates hesitation in the market.

That was the biggest surprise — the numbers that were thrown around. It will help the economy for sure, and we are one of the pillars trying to make sure that this expansion actually happens. But how do you get there?
CNN sues Perplexity

CNN sued Perplexity AI on Thursday, alleging the chatbot search engine illegally copies and uses the news outlet’s trademarks and copyrighted work to generate answers for users.

The lawsuit is the latest one filed by news outlets, publishers and other content owners alleging that AI companies unlawfully use copyrighted content from the internet to power their generative AI products.

CNN’s case alleges Perplexity engages in “large-scale and unlawful copying and distribution,” sometimes providing verbatim copies of its paywalled articles. The search engine also uses CNN’s logos, falsely suggesting an affiliation that harms the brand when Perplexity produces hallucinated answers, the lawsuit said.

“The public rely on high quality news journalism reported by human beings to understand their world, which is frequently dangerous and expensive to produce,” a CNN spokesperson said. “Commercial operators can and must pay to make use of it,” whether through licensing arrangements or legal damages.

The complaint, which was filed in federal court in New York, adds that Perplexity is knowingly misusing CNN’s materials because a content-sharing deal the two companies had been negotiating over ultimately fell through.

Perplexity rejected the allegations Friday. “You can’t copyright facts,” a company spokesperson told POLITICO.

Perplexity is facing similar lawsuits from The New York Times, Chicago Tribune and Encyclopedia Britannica. Amazon has sued the startup to block its AI bots from scraping up information from its online storefront.

Politico is part of a group of plaintiffs suing AI startup Cohere for similar alleged copyright and trademark violations.

CNN is represented by Rothwell, Figg, Ernst & Manbeck, which also represents the New York Times in copyright actions against OpenAI and Microsoft.
U.S. needles German streaming legislation

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer attacked a legislative proposal in Germany that would require streaming services like Netflix to invest in local media, POLITICO’s Milena Wälde reports.

The draft law, which the Cabinet of Chancellor Friedrich Merz approved on Wednesday, would oblige broadcasters and streaming companies to invest at least 8 percent of their annual revenues from Germany into domestic and broader European film and television projects. Greer said such a law would violate a trade pact that President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen struck in 2025 while in Turnberry, Scotland, which the EU agreed to implement last week.

“If this tax on American companies is enacted, it would be at odds with the Turnberry Agreement, in which the European Union committed to ‘address unjustified digital trade barriers’ — not erect new ones,” Greer said. Wolf Osthaus, Netflix’s senior global affairs director in Germany, told AFP, “If regulation ultimately makes it harder to invest in ambitious projects and, as a result, fewer titles are produced overall, that benefits neither audiences nor the production location.” POLITICO’s Mickey Djuric also reported this month that Canadian regulators have ordered global streaming platforms to invest 15 percent of their revenues from the country in domestic TV.

item.title: Pat Gelsinger dishes on chips, Intel and Trump
item.description: Pat Gelsinger dishes on chips, Intel and Trump
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Former Intel CEO Patrick Gelsinger speaks prior to President Joe Biden's remarks at Intel Ocotillo Campus in Arizona in 2024. | Rebecca Noble/Getty Images

Pat Gelsinger was Intel’s CEO from 2021 to 2024, and served on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology in the Biden administration. He helped usher in the CHIPS and Science Act during his tenure at Intel, and was at the helm when the company suddenly found itself playing catch-up with Nvidia in the race to produce chips to power the artificial intelligence boom. 

Gelsinger is now a general partner at the venture firm Playground Global, where he helps manage a tech-focused portfolio that includes semiconductor, quantum and AI infrastructure companies. In advance of Playground’s America by Design Summit on Tuesday, he spoke with DFD about the debate over chip tariffs, and the Trump administration’s unorthodox move to take a stake in Intel. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

How would you compare the Biden administration’s chip policy with Trump’s? 

One of my proudest days was at the State of the Union with the CHIPS Act. Getting the bipartisan CHIPS Act through Congress under the Biden administration was awesome. [It was] simply such an important piece of legislation to start codifying the next era of industrial policy. But I was very disappointed with how slowly the CHIPS Act was implemented under that administration.

Under this administration [there is] a greater sense of urgency to make an impact — get monies deployed, get companies formed, build things that are important for this industry in the future.

What do you make of the Trump administration renegotiating a lot of the CHIPS Act deals that were made under Biden?

Many of the CHIPS Act grants were pushed out the door just before the end of the [Biden] administration. Two-and-a-half years were squandered. This administration basically came in and said, “They were just doing last-minute deals to essentially bind us.” In many cases, those have gone forward, but under the policies that this administration felt were more appropriate ways to see monies deployed. It's continuing in the same spirit, but doing it with a view of: “We can do it better and faster than the last administration.”

Do you think it was a good idea for the Trump administration to take a stake in Intel?

The mechanism is OK if it brings about the outcomes that one wants to see. We want to see Intel be a great semiconductor company again. If, in fact, it leads people to not do business with them, then that's not good. So far, it's working pretty well. The U.S. government has seen Intel's momentum rebuild. [With the government] as a stakeholder, clearly it brings more attention to the broader ecosystem.

Do you think this equity stake approach would work for other tech-related sectors, like rare earths mining?

It's hard to say how you use that mechanism to accomplish the objective when those big mining companies may or may not be interested in an equity role, and they're mostly not U.S.-based. It's difficult to say that is the right tool to accomplish all of your policy objectives. In other cases, there could be some exciting startup companies that need capital and have new approaches to rare earths, in which case [equity stakes] could be a pretty good tool.

The Trump administration is considering additional tariffs on chips — how do you strike a balance between reshoring manufacturing and having cost-effective chips for the AI industry?

We didn't lose our supply chains to Taiwan, China, Singapore, Korea and Japan overnight. This was a very long, slow sedimentation of supply chains in Asia under solid economic reasons. And if we want to reshore those critical supply chains, there has to be solid economics underneath it. If the cost of building in the U.S. is equal to the cost of building in Asia, the supply chains won't move — no amount of political will or industrial favor will bring them back.

There must be economic dislocation for major moves in the supply chain. Tariffs … create economic dislocation that drives a preference for an alternative supply chain. If we want to have supply chains brought back to the U.S., they must be economically superior to the supply chains through Asia. You have to take very aggressive actions to move supply chains.

Speaking of Asia, there have been some questions about Taiwan’s independence from China after Trump’s recent visit to Beijing. How should the U.S. navigate that conflict given our dependence on Taiwanese chip manufacturing?

Carefully. In the first quarter of this year, Taiwan's exports exceeded those of China to the U.S. for the first time in history. Economic analysis has suggested that a browning out of the supply chain [i.e. withholding chips from Taiwan] would have more economic impact to the world and to the US than the Great Depression.

They have three weeks of energy capacity on the island of Taiwan. Building more energy resilience is maybe the most important thing that Taiwan could be doing to help secure its position in the world supply chain. That said, I fundamentally believe we need more supply in the U.S. We simply cannot be this dependent on any one spot. That doesn't mean that we just move everything to the U.S. But as we've seen with critical minerals, when you end up with 90-plus percent of supply chain constriction in one location, it jeopardizes industrial and economic policy.

Utah’s new data center framework

Utah Gov. Spencer Cox signed an executive order on Friday to address concerns about data centers in the state, POLITICO’s Joel Kirkland reports.

The order instructs agencies to follow a policy framework to ensure that data centers won’t increase utility bills or use of water from the Great Salt Lake. It also seeks to advance rural job growth. The order doesn’t have a lot of details on how exactly to achieve these goals, but Cox, a Republican, asserted that state agencies should make sure that efforts to provide electricity for AI data centers don’t clash with economic and environmental priorities.

“Utahns deserve confidence that water resources, air quality, utility rates, wildlife, and quality of life will be protected,” Cox wrote in an X post. “This framework helps ensure that data center development aligns with Utah’s long-term interests and reflects Utah values.”

item.title: The Pope’s AI warning lands in Washington
item.description: The Pope’s AI warning lands in Washington
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Calder McHugh

Pope Leo XIV issued an encyclical on AI last week. | Tiziana Fabi/AFP via Getty Images

In Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on artificial intelligence, published last week, the head of the Catholic Church offered a warning about unfettered AI development.

“Technology is never neutral, because it takes on the characteristics of those who devise, finance, regulate and use it,” he wrote at the outset. “Therefore, the primary choice is not between a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ to technology, but rather between constructing Babel or rebuilding Jerusalem; between a power that claims to dominate the heavens and a people who work together in the presence of God to rebuild the walls of fraternal coexistence.”

For 1.3 billion Catholics around the world, his missive holds significant moral authority. It also articulates a truth familiar to anyone who follows American politics: Nothing, and no one, is ever neutral.

And among people of faith with strong ties to Silicon Valley, no one faces a thornier dilemma when confronting Leo’s encyclical than Vice President JD Vance.

The country’s most powerful Catholic, Vance is also surely aware of growing AI skepticism on the religious right. At the same time, he has championed President Donald Trump’s broadly hands-off approach to AI and is a longtime Peter Thiel ally. In the days leading up to the release of the encyclical, the vice president was being pressed on it by reporters at a White House press briefing. 

As a leading contender for the 2028 GOP nomination, there was always going to be plenty of scrutiny of Vance’s AI stance. But his ties to both Silicon Valley and the Catholic Church have raised the stakes for his approach to the technology.

It also seems Vance’s approach may be shifting. After seeing the Anthropic model Mythos, which has yet to be released due to security concerns, Vance reportedly told an assembled group of AI CEOs on a call last month that it scared him, and that they needed to “work together” on the best way forward for the industry. 

That’s a very different message from a year earlier, when he said in a landmark speech in Paris that “we believe that excessive regulation of the AI sector could kill a transformative industry just as it’s taking off.”

A Vance spokesperson declined to comment. Last week, the vice president told Air Force Academy cadets that he “endorse[d]” Pope Leo’s sentiment that “human beings [should] not outsource the most important moral decisions to digital technology.”

Vance was also largely supportive of the pope’s message in an interview with NBC, saying he was glad Leo issued the encyclical.

“What I read of it sounds very profound, and the sort of thing that you would expect and hope from a leader of the church,” he said.

Those comments were slightly more positive than his remarks to the press before the encyclical was released, when he said, “I’m sure it will contain a lot of insights, some of which I’ll probably agree with, some of which I may not. But I think that it’s going to be a very, very important document.”

Some Vance skeptics were not persuaded.

“I think that there is this impossibility that JD Vance is trying to do — courting the Silicon Valley right who got him to the dance and keeping the Catholic right, who’s going to be trying to get him to the presidency,” said Christopher Hale, who writes Letters from Leo, a left-leaning Substack about the pope and U.S. politics. “He has too many plates in the air.”

How Vance weaves together his relationship with the broader Christian right, the tech right and the people who move between those two worlds will be critical as the 2028 presidential primary campaign approaches. Both the pope’s missive and the consternation over the proposed executive order have kicked off another round of infighting between these two powerful constituencies that Vance is attempting to straddle.

Jon Stokes, a co-founder of an AI and media company who also studied early Christian history and apocalyptic literature at Harvard Divinity School and the University of Chicago, predicts the problem for Vance has more to do with the president than the pope.

“He’s probably more hamstrung by the Trump administration’s complex relationship with AI [than the Church’s],” he said. In fact, Stokes argued that both the pope and Thiel are concerned about how AI can lead to further centralization of power — and Vance’s response to the question of centralization will be key.

It might not be so simple for him to align himself with the Church because of his role in government. 

“I think that if he wraps himself too much in the garment of the Catholic Church, then he risks alienating some portion of the electorate that he is going to need for his own political ambitions,” said Stephen Schneck, a Catholic activist who is the former chair of the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom and a political ally of former President Joe Biden.

At the same time, as news of the encyclical has rippled throughout Silicon Valley and beyond over the past week, the Church has emerged as an increasingly influential voice in an AI debate that extends well beyond matters of faith. AI poses moral problems that serious people of faith have considered for a long time. According to Charles Camosy, a professor of moral theology and bioethics at the Catholic University of America and a Catholic religious leader himself, this is a moment in which the world is ready to engage with the Pope in an expanded way.

“I really think this provides a moment, a new moment, for religious discourse in public,” he said. “It is astonishing that Leo is being taken so seriously on this question even as he is being so theological. It’s not watered down, warmed over pablum. It is deeply, deeply theological.”

Trump signs an AI executive order

President Donald Trump issued a scaled-back executive order Tuesday to address the cybersecurity threats posed by powerful new AI models, POLITICO’s Sophia Cai and Cheyenne Haslett were the first to report.

The order, signed privately, asks companies to submit powerful new models to a voluntary review 30 days before releasing them to the public, a move that would allow the government to evaluate what kinds of threats the tools pose to sensitive financial, national security and computer systems. An earlier draft called for a voluntary review 90 days before releasing a model. Trump planned to sign that earlier draft in May before calling off the ceremony at the last minute over concerns it would “get in the way” of U.S. competition with China over AI.

A White House official floated the idea of requiring federal approval for model releases in early May, sparking backlash from the industry and former Trump AI czar David Sacks.

The order also calls for officials at the Treasury Department, National Security Agency, the National Institute of Standards and Technology and other federal entities to establish a benchmarking process in the next 60 days to evaluate the cyber capabilities of AI models.

It also directs the Treasury Department to coordinate with other agencies and AI industry officials to establish a clearinghouse within 30 days. That initiative will involve a voluntary partnership with AI developers and owners of crucial infrastructure to identify and patch cybersecurity gaps. The NSA, Office of the National Cyber Director and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will also be involved in the effort.

EU executive to pitch Pax Silica

The European Union’s executive body will recommend that the bloc join a U.S.-led initiative known as Pax Silica to fortify AI supply chains, POLITICO’s Pieter Haeck reports.

A preparatory document obtained by POLITICO for a Wednesday meeting with EU ambassadors states that the European Commission “considers that the EU, represented by the Commission, should join Pax Silica as a signatory member.”

Pax Silica is aimed at expanding collaboration between the U.S. and allied countries on chips, critical minerals and AI models. The EU did not initially join Pax Silica when the U.S. launched the initiative in December, though Sweden and Finland signed up individually. The European Commission's recommendation may be in tension with its other plans for a tech sovereignty package to reduce the EU’s reliance on Silicon Valley.

item.title: AI’s ‘Big Tobacco’ danger
item.description: AI’s ‘Big Tobacco’ danger
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a complaint against OpenAI concerning the safety of ChatGPT on Monday. | Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images

A deluge of lawsuits accusing social media companies of harming young users is a flashing-red danger sign for the artificial intelligence industry.

Florida Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman on Monday, alleging in part that ChatGPT is a dangerous product for users’ mental health and public safety.

The suit is a novel use of product liability law for AI — but it parallels a legal strategy that plaintiffs are wielding in thousands of cases against major social platforms this year. The approach also echoes the wave of litigation by almost every U.S. state against the giant tobacco companies that led to multibillion-dollar settlements and restrictions on cigarette marketing in the 1990s.

A New Mexico jury held Meta liable in March for failing to implement sufficient safeguards against sexual predators, and a jury in California soon after found that Meta and YouTube had intentionally designed their platforms to be addictive.

Uthmeier’s lawsuit now has AI companies worried that social media’s “Big Tobacco” moment is coming for them as well.

“There is concern [among AI companies] about what happens with this product liability approach,” said Michelle Lopes Maldonado, associate director of AI policy at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation — a think tank whose funders include AI developers like Anthropic and Alphabet. “The possibility of multiplying suits by state attorneys generals could be real.”

Users and their families have already brought a handful of cases against AI chatbot companies for purported mental health harms, but Uthmeier is the first attorney general to do so. Matthew Bergman, an attorney representing the alleged victims in the California social media addiction case and separate chatbot litigation as the founder of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called Uthmeier’s involvement a major step for the kids online safety movement.

“What we have learned in the social media litigation is that the efforts of state AGs are complementary to the efforts of individuals in trying to hold these platforms accountable,” Bergman told DFD.

Yet some key differences between AI chatbots and traditional social media platforms could be relevant to courts, particularly when it comes to speech laws.

Social media companies have sought to win dismissal of many online safety suits under Section 230, the 1996 regulation that shields online platforms from liability for user-posted content. Some lower courts have found that Section 230 doesn’t apply to the current wave of cases because the allegations concern how the platforms are designed, rather than what users post — though the issue is sure to come up on appeal.

AI companies may have a weaker Section 230 claim, Maldonado said, because the chatbot is producing the speech.

From a product liability perspective, the challenges facing plaintiffs may be even more pronounced when it comes to AI.

One reason: Many recent social media lawsuits have relied on studies about the platforms’ mental health impacts, but the scientific literature on that topic is less definitive than the body of research linking cigarettes to cancer. (That uncertainty led to arguments in Meta and YouTube’s California trial concerning whether factors like a parent’s divorce could be the primary cause of a user’s mental health problems.) And even less research exists on the impacts of AI.

“In the social media case, we have lots and lots of social science research at least,” said University of Florida media law professor Jane Bambauer. “In the [AI] case, we have almost nothing, and the models keep changing.”

But Carrie Goldberg, a longtime tech safety advocate and attorney who is bringing product liability claims against xAI, said chatbots may have a clearer link to a user’s mental health travails given the interactive nature of the technology.

“We have somebody like a teenager using the AI bot as their therapist and confidant talking about suicide, and then it's coaxing them into suicide, [and] in the next moment they die,” Goldberg told DFD. “It's much easier to make the causal connection between the conduct that's happening with the generative AI and the harm.”

Some people on both sides of these chatbot debates hope to prevent a Big Tobacco moment from happening for AI.

“Social media companies had a 15-year run of addicting and harming kids before people really realized what was going on,” Bergman told DFD. “It is my hope and expectation that through early legal intervention, the [AI] industry can course correct.”

The AI companies are also looking to avoid the difficult legal debates that a Big Tobacco moment could entail. Maldonado told DFD the industry hopes national legislation will set ground rules for how companies should safely operate AI chatbots. The lack of federal guidelines for social media companies helped set the stage for the current wave of litigation.

“What we have to figure out is a federal standard sufficient enough to protect against the harms that should be reasonably foreseeable,” Maldonado said. “Technology moves at the speed of light, so we'll never keep pace, but what we can do is respond appropriately and iterate the guardrails as the technology evolves.”

OpenAI and the Florida attorney general’s office did not reply to requests for comment.

AI executive order is a win for safety advocates

So-called AI safety advocates are optimistic that President Donald Trump’s executive order signed on Tuesday opens the door to even stricter regulation of the technology, POLITICO’s Brendan Bordelon, Jacob Wendler and Gabby Miller report.

The order establishes a regime in which AI companies can voluntarily submit powerful models to the government to test for cybersecurity risks up to 30 days prior to release. Those pushing for more rigorous oversight of AI see the order as setting the stage for eventually requiring government evaluation before model releases.

“For the first time it's on a piece of paper, a structure and a process,” former Trump adviser Steve Bannon told POLITICO. “That process is still pretty ill-defined, it doesn't meet our requirements. But as I tell people, we’re going to eat the elephant one bite at a time.”

Caleb Knapp, senior policy manager at the Alliance for Secure AI, said the order provides Congress with “both an opportunity and responsibility to take this directive one step further and require AI developers to share their models for review before release.”

The European Parliament ditches Google

The French search engine Quant will replace Google as the European Parliament’s default search tool on Thursday, POLITICO’s Milena Wälde and Pieter Haeck report.

POLITICO viewed an email to lawmakers announcing that the swap is being made “in line with the Parliament’s commitment to digital sovereignty and the protection of users’ personal data.” The email characterizes Quant as a “privacy-focused European search engine” designed not to track users or harvest personal data.

The change coincides with a package of measures introduced on Wednesday to minimize the European Union’s dependence on foreign technology providers.

item.title: When tech politics become a financial risk
item.description: When tech politics become a financial risk
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Google's logo at the company's headquarters in Mountain View, California. | Marco Jose Sanchez/AP

The tech industry’s alignment with President Donald Trump is driving a growing political split between employees and executives.

There’s been a flurry of activism among tech workers pushing their bosses to cancel contracts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and to stop providing the Pentagon with AI for military applications.

Shareholders are increasingly involved in those internal fights — particularly over conflicts in the Middle East. A group of roughly 60 Microsoft investors owning $80 million in shares presented a proposal in July to rework the company’s due diligence procedures following reports that Israel was using its technology for mass surveillance and to identify targets in Palestine. Though the proposal failed, Microsoft has since discontinued certain services for Israel’s military.

Investors in Alphabet, Google’s parent company, are set to do something similar this week. A group of more than 40 investors holding about $2.2 billion in shares will present a resolution asking the board of directors to release a public report on how the company’s services may enable surveillance, censorship and military operations. The resolution mentions Project Nimbus, a contract Google and Amazon struck with Israel to provide cloud and AI technology.

Google insiders supporting this effort told DFD their success may hang on the controversy becoming a liability for investors. The hope is that shareholder and worker activism will feed off of each other to heighten the financial risks of Google’s involvement in global conflicts.

The overall effort may speak to the extent to which political considerations need to be translated into financial ones for tech industry activism to succeed.

“Nothing in that proposal needs one to be politically minded to accept [it],” said John Palowitch, a former researcher at DeepMind — Google’s AI lab — who will be presenting the resolution to the board at the company’s annual general meeting on Friday. “[The] proposal is completely 100% about the financial risk to the company and the bottom line.”

Employee opposition to Google’s work with governments has been escalating. Nearly a thousand Google workers signed an open letter calling for ethical red lines around the Pentagon’s use of the company’s technology amid the Iran war. (Google has roughly 190,000 employees in total.) London workers at DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, voted to unionize last month in part to organize against the company’s contracts with the U.S. and Israeli militaries.

Matthew Tschiegg, a Google cloud computing engineer who’s part of a campaign to end Project Nimbus, told DFD that the prospect of employees unionizing to oppose government contracts could go a long way toward swaying investors who may otherwise be indifferent to the politics of the matter.

“A shareholder or a fund that really doesn't care about the governance aspect may see that coordination and cohesion of U.K. DeepMind [employees] as a risk to the underlying stock and itself — even if they don't care about the harm that the software may be contributing to,” Tschiegg said.

There may also be external financial consequences to Google’s involvement in global conflicts, which activists are seeking to highlight. “Iran has threatened to target Google infrastructure in the latest war because they realize that Google is wrapped up as a military contractor for the U.S. and for Israel,” said Palowitch. “The [United Nations] has officially called Alphabet out for its contracts, and that can bring real future consequences.”

The government contracts at stake, however, are quite lucrative. The Project Nimbus contract, which Google and Amazon jointly entered into with Israel, is worth $1.2 billion. Google also has a $200 million contract with the Pentagon to provide AI tools, and has been awarded more than $7.9 million from U.S. immigration enforcement agencies since 2023.

Yet Joshua Brockwell, a communications director at Azzad — an investment firm that’s joined Friday’s resolution — told DFD that activist shareholders are trying to convince others that focusing on the immediate profits from those contracts might understate the longer-term risk.

“Just reputationally, it's a long-term problem — and [with] the entanglement and geopolitical conflict more broadly, we're not properly assessing or valuing these risks,” said Brockwell. “At some point, there has to be a reckoning when it comes to political, or legislative or judicial prosecutions, and that's a risk for the company.”

The shareholder resolution itself is on shaky ground, which even its supporters acknowledge. “It's not about the resolution technically passing … it's about the signal that this is sending to the board,” said Marcela Pinilla, sustainable investing director at Zevin Asset Management — which is leading the resolution. She added that there are “headwinds” to getting the proposal passed due to “institutional inhibition, the political pressure, and also the fact that data privacy, data governance in this age of surveillance is a novel issue.”

Alphabet’s board of directors has advised shareholders to vote against the proposal on the grounds that the company already has robust risk assessments and technical safeguards to address the concerns. Alphabet has a dual-class stock structure, which effectively gives the higher-ups veto power over resolutions.

“Obviously it will fail,” Brockwell told DFD. “It's a victory regardless because it's being talked about — we're having this conversation, other investors are having this conversation. Ideally, it will rise to the policy level, and we'll see change.”

Google did not respond to a request for comment.
Five Eyes warns of LinkedIn espionage

Spy agencies from the Five Eyes released a rare joint bulletin on Wednesday warning that Chinese intelligence operatives are using job platforms like LinkedIn and Indeed to recruit and compromise government personnel, POLITICO’s Mason Boycott-Owen reports.

Intelligence agencies from the U.S., the U.K., Canada, Australia and New Zealand found instances of people handing over sensitive information due to the espionage tactic, which has resulted in criminal prosecutions. The bulletin notes that Chinese operatives have posed as human resources professionals, consultants and think tank employees.

According to the joint statement, the spies from China “ultimately seek to acquire privileged military, political and economic intelligence that can provide China with a strategic and tactical advantage over the Five Eyes.”
FISA warnings

Sen. Ron Wyden is calling on senators to look over classified material detailing “serious abuses” of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, POLITICO’s Alfred Ng reports.

In a Wednesday letter, which POLITICO exclusively obtained, Wyden (D-Ore.) informed colleagues that he submitted classified documents to a secure Senate office for review regarding an opinion from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court on the alleged abuses. He urged lawmakers to review the submission prior to an upcoming vote on whether to renew FISA.

“There is clear evidence that Donald Trump and his administration are already abusing Section 702 in other ways,” Wyden wrote. “The category of warrantless searches that includes American politicians, activists and journalists more than tripled in 2025 and the FBI has refused to explain why.”

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told POLITICO, “Holding FISA hostage puts America’s national security at risk and it is shameful that some Democrats are threatening to put partisan politics ahead of the safety of the American people.”

item.title: 5 Questions for Louise Pentland
item.description: 5 Questions for Louise Pentland
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Louise Pentland | Adobe handout.

As Adobe’s chief legal officer, Louise Pentland has led the company’s global efforts to navigate the sea change that AI has set off in intellectual property, the creative economy and tech governance. Pentland has become a key advocate for the CREATOR Act — a bipartisan bill introduced this week that would give artists control over how their distinctive creative styles are used by AI to produce new works. She talks to us about the prospect of people living 150 years, and the rapid progress of open-weight models.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Creativity itself. We often talk about AI infrastructure — chips, models, compute — but the creative economy is foundational infrastructure too. It does not get the limelight in the same way. AI only becomes valuable because of the work, the content, the imagination, the style that's created. Without [the creative economy], it's a fairly significant missing piece. And when you consider that the creative economy contributes $1.2 trillion annually to the U.S. economy, that seems a very good reason to be paying close attention to it

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

Humanoid robots. I love the idea of it. I could use a few around my house. The commercial reality, the cost, reliability — it'll get there, but it's not there right now. And I think it's a little bit overhyped. It kind of segues into the idea that we can suddenly use AI just to replace all human activity. AI is a collaboration tool — it allows you to expand the art of the possible.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

We need to modernize the protections in this creative economy that we all live in [with] this AI era. The government could really be focused on protection, clarity, and control. It's one of the reasons why we are big supporters of the CREATOR Act … because it's a very thoughtful blend of the policy that we need in that sense. It protects human creators against AI-driven style impersonations, while preserving space for innovation and real legitimate creative expression. That's in part what we’re missing in this dialogue right now and why this fills a gap at this moment. Having a federally based rule on this will be a very important step forward.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Lifespan: Why We Age — and Why We Don't Have to by David Sinclair. It's sort of breaking the mold on what you could do with what we already have. It’s about new innovation and new inventions that have come out, or that are on the cusp of becoming readily accessible, to make you think about how you can leverage science and medicine in a way that is fundamentally healthy and beneficial. The idea that you could live until you were 150 in today's times is probably quite horrifying. The idea that you could live to 150 and be healthy, capable, with your organs still working and a great quality of life — that's not a fallacy anymore. We have the capabilities to do that. It's about how do we piece all of those together? It's medicine, science and technology coming together in a way we haven't seen.

What has surprised you the most this year?

Open-weight models. I think back to where we were a year ago. We were really struggling with how we're going to get access to weights, how we're going to be able to fine-tune [models]. What's been nicely surprising is how [open-weight models] have gotten closer to frontier closed models and capability through things like permissive licenses — Apache 2.0 is an example of that.

Also, a pleasant surprise is the fact that legal and regulatory actions are starting to catch up.

[The CREATOR Act] is one thing we're optimistic will start to have real concrete impact on things like AI copyright and AI protections after many years of this lagging behind the technology.
Polymarket recruits influencers

Polymarket has been paying at least two dozen influencers to hype up the prediction platform in social media posts that do not disclose the financial partnerships, POLITICO’s Jason Beeferman, Maya Kaufman, Jessie Blaeser and Declan Harty report.

Records reviewed by POLITICO indicate that Polymarket chief marketing officer Matthew Modabber sent at least $350,000 to content creators between January 2025 and February 2026. Many of the creators have large political followings on both sides of the aisle, and include progressive commentator Brian Krassenstein and Fox News contributor Riley Gaines. The content, which has been posted to platforms such as Instagram and X, have generally focused on the purported accuracy of Polymarket’s prediction odds for events like the 2025 New York City mayoral election and government shutdowns.

“We routinely collaborate with a diverse range of independent organizations, partners and content creators spanning the political spectrum and constantly monitor, evaluate our progress and make the necessary adjustments in order to achieve our core mission of providing the most accurate, transparent, and data-driven market insights to a global audience,” a Polymarket spokesperson told POLITICO. Modabber, Krassenstein and Gaines did not respond to requests for comment.
Bipartisan AI deal is on the rocks

Skepticism from key Democrats and Republican leadership threatens to tank a bipartisan bill to establish nationwide AI safety and transparency standards, POLITICO’s Brendan Bordelon, Meredith Lee Hill and Kelsey Brugger report.

Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) unveiled a draft Thursday of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, which would, in part, require AI developers to institute safeguards against catastrophic risks posed by advanced models, and enlist third parties to audit compliance with their measures.

Yet there is growing opposition among Democrats to provisions that would preempt state AI regulations for three years. Republicans have voiced concerns about working with Democrats on a potentially overburdensome federal framework. “You also don’t want to have some big regulatory structure at the federal level trying to control algorithms of private companies,” said House Majority Leader Steve Scalise. Democrats may be wary of bipartisan collaboration too. “Democrats are optimistic enough about taking the House that they’re not going to be striking any bipartisan deal between now and the [midterm] election,” said Chamber of Progress founder and CEO Adam Kovacevich.

item.title: The white-collar recession AI could create
item.description: The white-collar recession AI could create
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By John Hewitt Jones

With help from John Hendel

Headshot of Rise of the Robots author Martin Ford. | Xiaoxiao Zhao

Martin Ford is a futurist and author focused on the impact of artificial intelligence, automation, and robotics on the economy and workforce. A former computer engineer and software entrepreneur, Ford spent more than 25 years working in technology before turning to writing and research. He is the bestselling author of Rise of the Robots: Technology and the Threat of a Jobless Future, which won the Financial Times and McKinsey Business Book of the Year Award. A new edition of Rise of the Robots has just been published. Martin talks to us about the potential impacts of generative AI on the labor market.

Many economists have argued that AI would augment workers more than replace them. Has the widespread emergence of generative AI changed that balance?

Economists are certainly correct that past technological revolutions, like the introduction of steam engines, electricity or computers, increased the productivity of workers and ultimately led to more and better jobs for people. The key difference is that advanced AI is going to compete directly with the very thing that allowed us to adapt to new technologies in the past: our intelligence. In other words, AI will ultimately become a substitute for our cognitive capability, rather than something that augments it.

In particular, I think many economists have failed to really think through what the arrival of true human-level AI — artificial general intelligence or AGI — will mean. Tech leaders like Deepmind’s Demis Hassabis, who oversees all AI development at Google, are now predicting that AGI could well arrive by 2030 or shortly thereafter.

At a minimum, an AGI system will be equivalent to an extraordinarily smart and knowledgeable human sitting in front of a computer. The AGI will be able to do anything that person could do using the computer. It will be able to make calls and participate in Zoom sessions. It will be able to persuade, negotiate, and exercise judgement. It will be able to learn continuously, just as a human learns on the job. If the system can’t do those things independently and autonomously, then it is not AGI.

What's the biggest misconception policymakers or economists currently have about AI and the labor market?

Earlier this year, a small firm, Citrini Research, released a fictional scenario, “The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis,” that went viral and actually impacted the stock market. I was struck when I read it because the scenario it lays out is, in many ways, exactly what I have been warning of since I published my first book, The Lights in the Tunnel, in 2009. Rise of the Robots includes an entire chapter focused on the possibility of a crisis quite similar to the one described by Citrini.

As truly capable AI arrives, businesses across the economy have a powerful incentive to increase their profitability by replacing white-collar workers with AI. As this trend scales, this incentive rapidly evolves into a competitive necessity.

As more and more white-collar workers lose their jobs or fear becoming unemployed, they cut back on consumer spending. This will have a dramatic effect on the economy because highly-paid knowledge workers are among our most robust consumers. In the United States, the top 10 percent of households by income — those earning at least $250,000 per year—are responsible for fully half of all consumer spending. As high-income consumers cut their spending, the economy will spiral into a deepening recession. Many of these households will eventually struggle to pay mortgages and other loans, and this could potentially unleash a 2008-type financial crisis.

While I believe that such a scenario is quite plausible, most economists dismiss it out of hand. The noted economist Tyler Cowen, for example,recently told a gathering of OpenAI employees that the Citrini scenario is “impossible.” That seems dangerously complacent. Economists should engage with this idea with an open mind.

Which occupations are most vulnerable to being replaced by AI by 2030?

Among white-collar occupations, the early impact will be on jobs that are tightly bound to the digital world and, especially, where the tasks undertaken by workers have an objective outcome that can be verified through computation. Examples are software developers, financial or quantitative analysts, or call center workers (where there is a huge database of previous customer interactions). Lawyers who primarily write briefs based on existing case law or develop contracts are another example.

The field of robotics is also progressing rapidly, and this will have an impact on blue-collar workers in more controlled environments like warehouses and factories.

As most people have now recognized, the safest jobs are those that require extreme mobility, dexterity, visual/spatial perception and problem-solving ability in highly unpredictable environments. Plumbers, electricians and nurses will be safe until we have a robot like C3PO from Star Wars. I think that remains far off—but it will arrive eventually.

Are we overestimating the short-term disruption from AI, or underestimating it?

I think it’s quite likely that the common observation known as Amara’s Law, “We tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run” will apply to AI.

This is one reason I’m not a fan of precise predictions like the one made by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2025: AI could automate half of entry-level white-collar jobs, and cause unemployment to reach 10-20 percent in the next one to five years.

While I certainly agree with this in spirit, no one can predict with any confidence exactly what the timeframe or the future unemployment rate will be. My argument is that automation from advanced AI is inevitable at some point. But if we promise a specific timeframe and those years pass without the job losses occurring, people will likely become dismissive and complacent.

Should firms deploying AI at scale bear some responsibility for helping workers displaced by the technology?

Ultimately, I think this is a collective action problem that can only be addressed through government policies. However, the AI firms and the business community at large should certainly play a role in advocating for and helping to craft such policies. It is very much in the self-interest of large corporations and small businesses alike to support policies that maintain consumer demand in the face of job automation.

Every business needs demand for its products and services, and ultimately, this demand comes from consumers. This is true even for businesses that sell to other businesses. Boeing and Airbus will not sell aircraft if the airlines that are their customers do not see demand for plane tickets.

What aspects of the AI boom are likely to have the most profound effect on society in the coming decades?

I’ve already talked at some length about AI risks, especially job automation and the resulting impact on the economy, and I believe this will certainly be part of the story in the coming decades. I remain a strong proponent of progress in AI.

Everything that human beings have ever created — including our entire civilization — is a direct result of our intelligence. Intelligence is the ultimate resource, and we are entering an age when that resource will exist in unprecedented abundance. That will allow possibly unimaginable progress in science, technology and medicine. AI will be indispensable in solving our most difficult challenges, including global poverty, new energy sources and climate change.

However, that positive future will only unfold if we can adapt our system to address the new economic and social realities that AI will bring about. So, I think it is important to have an open mind about the changes that may be coming and put real effort into developing policies and strategies that will allow us to adapt. This is not a time to be complacent that the old rules will always and everywhere continue to apply.

item.title: China is closing in on America’s AI advantage
item.description: China is closing in on America’s AI advantage
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Maggie Miller and Dana Nickel

Chinese and U.S. flags wave in Beijing on April 17, 2025. | Pedro Pardo/AFP via Getty Images

Silicon Valley has kept the U.S. at the forefront of technological innovation for decades, including the advent of artificial intelligence models with hacking capabilities, such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos.

But as China and other potential adversaries race to acquire similar technology and shape a new era of cybersecurity, the U.S. is at risk of losing its control over how these AI tools are used.

Some recent estimates suggest that the U.S. has at most six to 12 months before Beijing gains access to a frontier model comparable to Mythos or OpenAI’s GPT 5.5-Cyber — which can find exploits in virtually any network — or develops an AI competitor that could eventually be wielded as a cyber weapon.

This gap is shrinking by the day — and may have shrunk to hours on Tuesday, with the release by Anthropic of Claude Fable 5, what the company described as “Mythos-class model that we’ve made safe for general use.” This could allow cyber professionals in other nations, such as China, to test a watered-down version of Mythos — previewing the still gated Mythos.

“It's a hurricane warning, not a seawall,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer at cybersecurity research company the SANS Institute, said of the limited time the U.S. has to prepare before this new wave of hyper-advanced AI models changes the cybersecurity calculus entirely.

Both Anthropic and OpenAI initially limited testing of their newest AI models to a small group of trusted defenders when the models were first announced in April, as the companies weighed the immense consequences of the technology’s wider release. Anthropic gave another 100  organizations in more than a dozen nations access to Mythos earlier this month — excluding China.

China reportedly asked Anthropic to trial Mythos in May, but was rebuffed. Two days later, Anthropic published a blog post in which the company noted that “it’s essential that the U.S. and its allies stay ahead of authoritarian governments like the Chinese Communist Party.”

Despite these guardrails, China will almost certainly still gain access to these or similar AI models, particularly after the release of Fable 5.

“There is some balance point between limited availability and broad availability that needs to be found so that we can collectively find and fix as much of the critical products out there as possible before the attackers get their hands on these models,” said Lee Klarich, chief product and technology officer at cyber firm Palo Alto Networks.

The Trump administration and Congress alike are weighing how to support the continued development of American-made technology while balancing the need for greater guardrails.

Despite tensions between AI accelerationists and security advocates slowing down action, President Donald Trump signed an executive order last week that encourages AI companies to submit their powerful new models for voluntary government review at least 30 days before releasing them to the public. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is expected to direct federal agencies this week to boost their security against new AI threats.

This call to action has extended to Capitol Hill. Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) unveiled a 269-page draft bill last week that would include regulations around AI safety and security, along with a three-year ban on state laws related to AI. The bill is unlikely to make it to Trump’s desk in its current form due to objections over the state law preemptions — but many still view it as a positive first step for Congress.

Whether these actions will be enough to stave off China’s attempts to surpass U.S. AI technology remains uncertain, particularly as Beijing increasingly focuses on the issue. The Chinese government recently made the integration of AI into its economy a major part of its five-year plan to grow its scientific and technological dominance.

Meanwhile, Chinese AI companies like DeepSeek are reportedly trying to raise billions in funding for “groundbreaking AI research” and to better compete with U.S. frontier labs. And Beijing is reportedly pursuing deeper cooperation with the Russian government on AI and cybersecurity, raising alarm among U.S. defense strategists about their efforts to forge a new world order with powerful technologies in hand.

Evan Peña, founder and chief offensive security officer at AI security company Armadin, suggested that the Chinese government and other groups are likely already using DeepSeek’s latest V4 model to achieve results similar to those of Mythos and GPT-5.5-Cyber.

“Mythos costs a good amount of money to run from a token consumption perspective and compute time,” Peña said. “DeepSeek Version 4 … it’s 20x cheaper than [Anthropic’s] Opus 4.8, it’s probably 30x cheaper than something like Mythos.”

Lee of the SANS Institute stressed that defenders should use advanced AI to find and patch vulnerabilities in critical systems before the clock runs out.

“You have time to board up and move what matters,” Lee said. “But the storm will land, and you need to make sure you aren't just standing out in the yard when it does.”

Catch up on Season 1 featuring Josh Shapiro, Wes Moore, JB Pritzker, Brian Kemp, Gavin Newsom and more on American politics, the road to 2026 and what’s next. Watch Season 1 now.

 
 
AI bill faces House reality check

Rep. Jay Obernolte has an aggressive timeline for getting his new bipartisan Artificial Intelligence proposal taken up in the House, which includes turning his draft into multiple bills, POLITICO’s Kelsey Brugger reports.

“One of the challenges that we have is that the bill crosses so many different policy committee jurisdictions,” said the California Republican. “So I think we’ve got to divide it up into different titles that are in the jurisdiction of various policy committees and hear those individually.”

Obernolte said most of the provisions fall under the purview of the Committee on Science, Space and Technology, including language authorizing the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and the National AI Research Resource.

But the biggest obstacle facing Obernolte and his Democratic co-sponsor, Rep. Lori Trahan of Massachusetts, remains getting buy-in from their respective leadership and colleagues, all of whom are divided on the bill and the role the federal government should play in regulating AI.

House Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu slammed the framework, saying it “cannot meet the enormity of the moment.”
Trump’s AI profit-sharing pitch splits Silicon Valley

President Donald Trump’s embrace of a potential financial partnership between the federal government and the artificial intelligence industry is dividing people in Silicon Valley on whether to pursue such a tight alliance with Washington.

The White House has yet to invite major tech companies to a meeting that the president had said could occur as early as this week, said three people familiar with the policy discussions and granted anonymity to describe them told POLITICO. Trump and his aides also haven’t spelled exactly how such a partnership would work.

The plan, though, is creating strange bedfellows in Washington, as Trump’s talk appears to align him with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who’s called for the government to take a large stake in AI companies’ stock to distribute the proceeds to Americans. Meanwhile, the tech giant OpenAI is also urging the government to redistribute its profits to the public.

“The White House, progressives in Congress and the industry itself may disagree sharply on the solution,” said Joseph Hoefer, principal and chief AI officer at the bipartisan lobbying firm Monument Advocacy. “But they’re responding to the same underlying worry: that AI could generate extraordinary value, and the public wants confidence it will share in the upside rather than just absorb the disruption.”

item.title: Wrongful arrest suit sparks fresh scrutiny of police facial recognition
item.description: Wrongful arrest suit sparks fresh scrutiny of police facial recognition
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng

With help from Gabby Miller

A live demonstration of artificial intelligence and facial recognition. | David McNew/AFP via Getty Images

Despite improvements in facial recognition software, police across the country are continuing to make wrongful arrests from the technology as lawmakers lag behind on setting safeguards.

The American Civil Liberties Union reported at least 15 documented cases of wrongful arrests from facial recognition misidentifying people since 2019, without any federal regulations setting standards on how the technology should be used.

Robert Dillon, a Florida man who was wrongly arrested after a facial recognition search misidentified him as a suspect in an investigation more than 300 miles from his home, filed a lawsuit on Wednesday to prevent police from making the same mistakes that he said ruined his life.

“I want to be compensated for what’s been done to me, but the biggest thing is, I don’t want it to happen to anybody else. I don’t wish this on my worst enemy,” Dillon told Digital Future Daily.

The lawsuit alleged that officers from the Jacksonville Beach Police Department, the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office and the Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office, did not take proper steps to prevent the wrongful arrest, including making sure the surveillance image used met minimum quality standards for a facial recognition search.

The investigating officer took a photo of surveillance footage from a McDonald’s, showing a suspect attempting to lure a minor to leave the fast food chain with him shortly before midnight. The photo of the surveillance footage — rather than the high resolution pictures from the video itself — was what ended up being entered into the facial recognition search, the lawsuit alleged.

Police arrested Dillon in August 2024, despite evidence from license plate readers showing that Dillon’s vehicles were not in the city at the time of the incident, and physical differences such as a scar and facial hair that were distinct from the suspect in the surveillance footage.

The Jacksonville Beach Police Department and the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office declined to comment. An attorney representing the Jacksonville Beach Police Department and the Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to a request for comment.

Dillon’s lawsuit is calling for financial compensation, and an order requiring the agencies to adopt and implement safeguards around its facial recognition use.

“Police departments have threadbare policies that they tell the public will protect people against misuse of this technology, but in fact they provide no meaningful guidance to officers and leave everybody vulnerable to police effectively blindly trusting this technology and letting incorrect results taint investigations,” Nathan Freed Wessler, the deputy director of the ACLU’s Speech, Privacy and Technology Project and Dillon’s attorney, told DFD.

The most significant changes in police use of AI over the last five years have come from lawsuits rather than legislators. A landmark settlement from the ACLU with Detroit following a wrongful arrest from facial recognition in 2024 established the nation’s strongest safeguards on police use of facial recognition, which Indiana adopted a version of in 2025.

Experts warn that police will continue to make wrongful arrests from facial recognition unless lawmakers pass regulations.

“Civil lawsuits are too far and few between to actually have systemic impact. You really need to have a legislative response to say we need rules in place to have consequences if you misuse it,” Andrew Guthrie Ferguson, a criminal law professor specializing in police surveillance technology at the George Washington University Law School, said.

Members of Congress have pushed to pass regulations in the past on facial recognition, though efforts usually do not make it far. Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) introduced legislation to put a moratorium on police use of facial recognition in 2023, but the bill did not make it out of committee.

“Americans should not have to live in fear that an unaccountable algorithm could put them in handcuffs. I will not allow this flawed technology to ruin lives,” he said in a statement to DFD.
META NOT FOCUSED ON TRUMP’S AI EQUITY STAKE IDEA

Meta is largely tuning out a suggestion from President Donald Trump that the U.S. government should forge a financial partnership with top artificial intelligence companies, our Brendan Bordelon reports.

“Honestly, it's just not something that I've spent — we've spent a ton of time on,” chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan said during POLITICO’s Energy Summit in Washington when asked about the notion of the federal government taking a "sizable equity stake” in Meta or other AI developers.

His comments come after Trump floated the idea last Friday of giving “pieces” of top AI firms to the American public, which the president suggested would “essentially becom[e] a partner with the companies.” While Trump did not name any companies, the leading AI companies in the U.S. include firms such as Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic.

Read the full piece from Brendan here.
HOUSE E&C CONSIDERS DATA CENTER REGS

House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie said he’s interested in moving forward with legislation to address the impact of data centers, our Manuel Quiñones reports from POLITICO’s Energy Summit.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill are divided on whether a new federal law is needed on the issue. But Guthrie, a Kentucky Republican, joined House leaders in promising action earlier this year following a push from the White House, which has extracted a pledge from companies to pay for their own energy use.

When asked about data center concerns Wednesday, Guthrie said, "We have the ratepayer protection pledge, which we want to put into statute."

Guthrie's referring to draft legislation called the "Ratepayer Protection Act," which his committee held a hearing on in April and would amend the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 to require large electricity users — such as data centers — to cover the full cost of the infrastructure needed to serve them.

item.title: The fight to prevent AI from setting your prices
item.description: The fight to prevent AI from setting your prices
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng

Shoppers shop at a grocery store in Schaumburg, Illinois, Feb. 9, 2026. | Nam Y. Huh/AP

A growing movement in state capitals is trying to get ahead of fears that artificial intelligence will soon be able to use troves of data on every American to pinpoint exactly how much someone is willing to pay for a gallon of milk or a plane ticket.

As concerns about the cost of living and anxieties about AI’s impact on everyday life continue to, rise, lawmakers are pushing regulations to prevent algorithms from using personal data gathered from mobile apps, web browsers and other online tools to automatically estimate the highest price a person is willing to pay.

New York and Connecticut last week joined Maryland in becoming the first states to pass laws on so-called surveillance pricing, with bills in New Jersey, Delaware and California being considered in the coming weeks and months.

Consumer advocates want a full ban on the use of personal data combined with AI to set individualized prices, while tech industry lobbyists are pushing their own legislation that still allows data for some uses, like providing personalized discounts.

No front-runner approach has emerged yet, as New York’s bill follows consumer advocates’ framework, Maryland’s regulations align with the tech industry’s push, and Connecticut lands in between the two.

“We expect policymakers to continue to grapple with this for a while,” Grace Gedye, a policy analyst at Consumer Reports, told Digital Future Daily.

Similar to how advocates and industry groups are pushing statehouses to pass their own versions of data privacy and AI regulations, the more states that adopt one approach, the more likely it is to become the national standard. Lobbyists are already pointing lawmakers toward Maryland’s model in legislative hearings.

“Other states that have acted in this area have focused on personalized price increases, while preserving consumer discounts and loyalty programs,” Jabari Cooper, the Northeast director of state and local government relations for the tech industry group Chamber of Progress, said at a hearing on Delaware’s surveillance pricing bill on Tuesday. “Maryland passed a surveillance pricing law this year, but it is carefully tailored to address only personalized price increases.”

Consumer advocates originally supported Maryland’s law, but criticized the legislation following a series of amendments that allowed companies to continue using personal data as long as it was for discounts.

They argue that the practice of using people’s data for personalized pricing — even if it is for discounts — still results in higher costs.

“If you get a deeper discount than me, I paid more than you. That’s no different than me getting charged more than you. The outcome is the same. You and I paid different prices for the same item at the same time, and it was based on personal information about us,” Lindsay Owens, the executive director of the progressive economic think tank Groundwork Collaborative, said to DFD.

Owens and other consumer advocacy groups are championing New York’s One Fair Price Act, which lawmakers passed on June 4 and is awaiting Gov. Kathy Hochul’s signing.

“That would be one of the biggest advances that we could see in protecting consumers from this swarm of price discrimination,” Owens said.

Hochul has until the end of the year to sign the bill; spokesperson Kassie White said the governor will review the legislation.

Tech industry groups argue that New York’s full ban on data-driven pricing hurts companies’ ability to offer discounts and raises costs for consumers. This argument has been effective in other states, as Connecticut’s bill skews closer to Maryland’s model and Colorado governor Jared Polis vetoed a similar bill on June 2 citing these concerns.

“Because of the broad sweep, the bill would punish differentially lower prices, not just higher prices,” Polis said in his veto letter.

Polis’ veto, and the amendments made to Maryland and Connecticut’s laws, help the tech industry make the case across statehouses.

“It’s worth pointing out that the only bills that have made it across the finish lines so far are the ones that have been more narrowly tailored to exempt discounts and pro-consumer practices,” Drew Ambrogi, the Chamber of Progress’ policy manager, told DFD.
DeSantis opposes Trump AI plan

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis criticized the White House’s efforts to block state regulations on AI on Thursday, calling it “amnesty for Big Tech.”

DeSantis has been one of the loudest Republican voices against President Donald Trump’s push to preempt state AI laws.

“Combined with a potential de facto bailout of OpenAI, it represents bad policy and even worse politics,” DeSantis said on social media in response to  POLITICO’s reporting about the White House’s plans to preempt state AI regulations.

DeSantis is not the only Florida politician going after the AI industry. State Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against AI company OpenAI on June 1.

Read the full report from POLITICO’s Andrew Atterbury.
Data center dilemma in battleground America

Data centers are planned for a majority of battleground House districts, sending a curveball for campaigns this midterm election, according to a new analysis from POLITICO.

Data centers have quickly become a heated political issue, and Democrats and Republicans are struggling to come up with a unified message as 40 out of 69 competitive districts have plans to build or already have data centers under construction, according to the analysis.

Five Republicans and one Democrat incumbent responded to POLITICO’s questions about their stance on data center regulations, highlighting voters’ concerns about rising costs from data centers. Read the full analysis from our colleagues Catherine Allen and Noah Baustin.
