item.title: Five questions for James Anderson
item.description: Five questions for James Anderson
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from John Hendel 

James Anderson | Bloomberg Philanthropies handout

James Anderson is the head of Bloomberg Philanthropies’ government innovation program, which works with cities around the world to implement data analytics, digital permitting, electric buses and other technologies. He also helps oversee the Mayors AI Forum, an initiative by Bloomberg Philanthropies and Johns Hopkins University that brings municipal governments and the tech industry together to shape how the technology is used in cities. Anderson previously served as the communications director for former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg. Anderson discusses where the smart cities movement went wrong, and how local governments get left out of the political discourse. 

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

The artificial intelligence edge in government won’t come from technology. It will come from institutional capacity.

Over the past decade, many mayors have quietly laid the foundation that effective use depends on: better information systems, stronger coordination across departments, clearer governance and public servants trained to use — and even love using — data. That preparation is why local governments from Boston to Bogotá to Nairobi are moving faster now. Building these capabilities inside city hall has been the focus of Bloomberg Philanthropies’ government innovation program for more than a decade.

The Mayors AI Forum takes that work upstream: bringing these officials — and the urban realities and residents they represent — into the policymaking and development decisions that will determine where this technology goes next.

What’s a technology that you think is overhyped?

Any tech that is deployed without a clear problem in view.

The most sophisticated public officials don’t start with new software and flashy tools. They begin with the challenge at hand. They use hard data, resident insights, and frontline perspectives to understand where systems break down and what people actually need. Then they build solutions backward from there, integrating technology where — and only where — it helps solutions move farther and faster.

That is what much of the smart cities movement got wrong. Technology is an enabler. It is not the point.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

The Ungovernable City: John Lindsay and His Struggle to Save New York by Vincent Cannato — which the legendary editor of the New York Post opinion page, Bob McManus, sent me when I started as communications director for Bloomberg. Cannato largely presents Lindsay’s mayoralty as a failure, but not a failure of ambition. Lindsay saw the city as the place where America’s hardest problems came home: race, poverty, crime, labor, bureaucracy and trust.

The lesson I took away was not that cities are ungovernable. It was that cities demand a more serious form of governing: more creative, more capable and more relentless about implementation. Vision without capacity is fragile. And that insight has shaped my work ever since — helping mayors build the capacity to match the scale of the problems they are brave enough to take on.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

Investing in the workforce that transformation demands. True 21st Century government requires reimagining how government works. That level of modernization can’t simply be outsourced. It’s an inside job — carried out by in-house engineers, designers, and programmers alongside agency leaders, frontline staff and policy chiefs. To succeed, governments need to upskill existing staff, strengthen digital fluency and recruit top technical talent into public service — all with the same national resolve that once put a man on the moon.

What has surprised you the most this year?

How mainstream “state capacity” has become in the national conversation — and how rarely that conversation centers on the level of government where it is often needed most. The good news is serious debates are now happening across the political spectrum. The abundance agenda, in particular, has made a compelling case that procedural complexity too often stands in the way of erecting the housing and infrastructure a thriving nation requires.

But our ability to build will not be determined in the abstract, or in Washington or state capitals. It will be determined by the capabilities of city halls, municipal departments, and public works offices in communities across the country.

Local government is the first and last mile of every major challenge and opportunity we face. National policy is only as effective as its implementation on the ground — a lesson we forget to our great detriment. If we want America to build, we must build municipal capacity to do the job.
SpaceX goes public

Today marked SpaceX’s debut on the stock market in the world’s largest initial public offering, fueling plenty of chatter about the future of Elon Musk’s rocket company. Its efforts are shaping many key tech world debates, from AI to satellite broadband to data centers — making Musk the world’s first trillionaire.

“Now it’s time to scale,” SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC.

SpaceX’s expansion, however, still comes with many open policy questions. Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, is among those questioning whether SpaceX’s public offering figures really added up.

In a recent research note, strategy firm Capstone noted that internet service Starlink is SpaceX’s most profitable endeavor but that Musk is more focused on orbital AI data centers. “Significant technological advancements will be necessary for orbital data centers to compete with terrestrial data centers, and no one knows whether they will succeed,” Capstone analysts wrote.

Others, meanwhile, fear SpaceX’s astronomical IPO adds pressure to a potential AI bubble (along with upcoming IPOs for OpenAI and Anthropic.)

“As things stand, the AI system is like a dazzling array of dominos — eye-catching and poised to topple with the slightest jostling,” MS NOW’s Hayes Brown wrote in an op-ed today. “Should one of these firms prove unable to meet the obligations it has to the other major players, the cascading effect could launch another recession.”
Schumer downbeat on AI deal

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wants Congress to pass legislation reining in artificial intelligence — but he’s not holding his breath for any breakthroughs in 2026.

“In this Congress, it’s hard,” Schumer told POLITICO in a recent interview.

Schumer’s blunt assessment of the prospects reflects the complexity of the AI legislative challenge. The central tech issue has dominated Washington for well over a year, and policymakers are struggling to strike the right balance between preempting state measures and which other issues to draw in, such as proposals to safeguard children’s online safety.

The New York Democrat, of course, spearheaded some major bipartisan talks about AI when he was majority leader in the previous Congress. He and colleagues from both parties frequently convened on how to tackle AI’s various dimensions and in mid-2024, his bipartisan working group unveiled a roadmap for how Congress might address the emerging tech.

And if Democrats regain the Senate after the November midterms, Schumer could step back into an even more dominant role in deciding what legislation looks like.

“We should get something done on AI, and it’s … got to be balanced — keep innovation strong, but have guardrails to prevent the dangers,” Schumer said. “That’s a hard needle to thread, but I would very much like to see that get done the sooner the better.”

item.title: Data centers are becoming a fixture of battleground politics
item.description: Data centers are becoming a fixture of battleground politics
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Catherine Allen

With help from Alfred Ng

A person walks near a data center in Sterling, Virginia, on March 9, 2026. | Francis Chung/POLITICO


The AI-driven data center boom is colliding with the politics of affordability, and House candidates are increasingly caught in the middle.

Across the country, data centers have become targets of community opposition to rising electricity bills, water consumption, land use and the influence of Big Tech. In Wisconsin, community dissent has disrupted five data center proposals. In Tennessee, residents clashed with local officials over Elon Musk's xAI data center. In Ohio, New York and more, proposals to ban the construction of new data centers are gaining traction.

Now, those fights are spilling into races that will decide control of the House in November.

A POLITICO analysis of Data Center Map data found that 40 of the 69 most competitive congressional districts have data centers planned or under construction. Nationwide, roughly 1,500 facilities are in development across 232 congressional districts, split almost evenly across Republican- and Democrat-held seats.

The scale of the buildout means lawmakers from Virginia’s data center-heavy suburbs to the industrial Midwest are confronting the same question: how do you embrace an industry tied to jobs, investment and the AI race without getting blamed for higher utility bills and other local impacts?

Even though Republicans represent most of those competitive districts, data centers are shaping up to be a yearslong political slog that neither party has an answer for.

Interviews and statements gathered by POLITICO from more than 20 congressional candidates, political strategists and activists make clear that while individual campaigns are trying to shape their positions, broader party messaging is essentially nonexistent. “There’s not one big national message on this specific thing,” said one Democratic strategist working on congressional races, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But in certain districts, data centers are going to be a major, major player.”

The political challenge is evident in how incumbents talk about the issue, with candidates in battleground states emphasizing the economic and national security benefits of data centers while stressing the importance of shielding consumers from costs associated with the buildout. Iowa Rep. Zach Nunn (R) — who represents a district with 31 data centers planned and 33 already operating — acknowledged in a statement how workforce development and AI leadership can work hand in hand, but said he hears from constituents who “don't want higher utility bills or sweetheart deals for out-of-state tech companies.”

Asked about its strategy on data centers, Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Viet Shelton said, “while House Republicans fall in line behind failed policies that spike prices out of control, Democratic candidates and Frontliners are fighting for common sense solutions to provide meaningful price relief, encourage economic growth, and meet the unique needs of their communities.” The National Republican Congressional Committee declined to comment.

Democratic Rep. Eugene Vindman of Virginia’s 7th district ranks the highest among competitive districts with the most upcoming data centers — those that are planned or under construction — followed by Nunn. When POLITICO asked the top 10 House members on that list about their stance on data center regulations, five of eight Republican incumbents, and one of two Democrats, responded. Their answers embraced data centers in the name of economic development and national security, but also illustrated an awareness that voters are in no mood to greenlight anything that will send electricity bills higher.

The attempt at striking a balance speaks to the tech lobby’s rising pressure in the midterm races. Candidates — particularly incumbents — who are too critical, run the risk of losing support from the tech lobby or attracting fierce opposition.

“They’re between a rock and a hard place,” said Texas-based GOP consultant Brendan Steinhauser, whose clients have included Sen. John Cornyn and Rep. Dan Crenshaw. “Politically, it’s not a very smart move to come out and be seen as too close to big tech or doing the bidding of big tech, but a lot of the money is flying to them through that.”

The advertising so far this election cycle backs that up. Among the congressional and gubernatorial ads that mention data centers, as identified by the political advertising tracker AdImpact, all of them are critical of the facilities. Most attack Republicans for supporting them.

The Data Center Coalition, an industry association, has supported the White House’s “ratepayer protection pledge” and other policies that require data centers to cover more utility costs. The coalition’s senior director of federal affairs, Cy McNeill, said that they’re working to educate representatives as constituents increasingly voice concerns about water usage and energy prices.

“How do we provide the facts to the office, or to the congresswoman or congressman, to kind of help educate constituents on this?” McNeill said. “If we actually take a step back, look at the facts, I think the story is a lot different.”

As the AI boom accelerates and the data center buildout continues, House candidates are largely being left to navigate the politics on their own — at least for now.

Florida turns up the heat on tech giants

TikTok allegedly exposed children to harmful content and incorporated addictive features into its social media platform in violation of a new Florida law, according to a lawsuit filed Monday.

The filing from Florida State Attorney General James Uthmeier accused TikTok of violating a law prohibiting anyone younger than 14 from being on a platform with infinite scrolling and push notifications, among other addictive features, according to POLITICO’s Andrew Atterbury.

TikTok could face billions of dollars in penalties in what Uthmeier called “one of the most egregious social media applications” for harming children. He said the state used undercover agents in its investigation against TikTok, and believes that children are using the app for more than eight hours a day.

TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit.
Survey puts China ahead of U.S. on AI

China has taken the lead as the world’s AI superpower, according to a poll surveying 18,000 people across 15 countries.

The majority of respondents in 11 countries — including U.S. allies such as France, the United Kingdom and Canada — considered China as the dominant global force in AI development, while respondents from Japan, Vietnam, India and the U.S. believed the U.S. is the global leader, our colleague Owen Dalhkamp writes.

The findings contradict American optimism on Silicon Valley’s AI growth, as President Donald Trump said last week that the U.S. was far ahead of China’s AI capabilities.

The poll also showed respondents believed the U.S. would continue to lag behind China’s AI development, with growing worries about AI’s effect on society.

The poll was conducted by Public First, which is not related to the Anthropic-backed political action group.

item.title: Why it’s hard to control software exports
item.description: Why it’s hard to control software exports
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The Trump administration imposed export controls on multiple Anthropic models last week. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

Restricting the distribution of computer programs has never been an easy task, but that isn’t stopping the Trump administration.

The White House imposed extensive export controls on Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 last week, which led the company to shut down all customer access to the models. Despite Anthropic’s assurances, senior officials developed fresh doubts that the systems’ safeguards against potentially dangerous uses aren’t adequately secure.

This isn’t the first time that the government has tried to impose export controls to keep high-risk software out of the wrong hands. In fact, there are controls in place for software used in missile systems, battle simulations and other defense applications.

Yet regulating software exports has proven to be a legal and logistical can of worms. Though AI is an exceptionally powerful and transformative technology, those attempting to regulate it with export controls may run into challenges encountered with other types of software.

“In general, controlling software is much harder than controlling hardware, and there's no reason that won't be true in this case,” said Michael Horowitz, a former deputy assistant defense secretary in the Biden White House.

The battle over exports of encryption technologies at the turn of the century is an instructive precedent for the current controversy around Anthropic. The Clinton administration pursued a variety of ultimately unsuccessful efforts to restrict the spread of code that encrypts communications, on the grounds that the software posed a threat to national security and law enforcement.

On a practical level, it proved to be difficult to restrict the flow of information on a borderless internet. In one case, the Clinton Justice Department sought to take legal action against the developer of an encryption program known as Pretty Good Privacy. By the time the department dropped the investigation, the software was already widely available on the internet.

While only the U.S.’ major frontier labs have so far created powerful models like Mythos, developers in other countries are expected to have their own versions in a matter of months. Open-source versions may also eventually make the technology more widely available.

“China has the leading open models, but is that something they continue to do as the models become more capable?” Brad Carson, president of the nonprofit Americans for Responsible Innovation, told DFD. He added that software export controls are unlikely to be effective by themselves, and would need to be paired with strong limits on chip sales abroad.

Since export controls were initially designed for the international circulation of physical items, they aren’t always the best fit for code. “For models that are publicly available, in some ways you have to almost assume some degree of leakage internationally, even if you have strong export controls,” said Horowitz.

And then there’s the potential constitutional hurdles. The Clinton State Department and DOJ suffered a major legal defeat in the landmark 1999 case Bernstein v. United States, which involved a Ph.D. student who challenged export controls on his encryption algorithm and source code.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals struck down the restrictions, holding that they infringed on the First Amendment. The ruling established that software can be considered speech in some instances, as developers often use code to express scientific ideas.

Courts are mulling over the question of whether AI chatbot algorithms are protected by the First Amendment in a number of pending cases, which could have implications for the export controls debate.

Carson contends, however, that there may be some legally salient differences between cryptographic and AI codes. The constitutional precedents around encryption are focused squarely on the code itself, while cases involving generative AI systems also concern whether outputs are a form of speech.

“If I write code, that's actually communicating my intent … it is me attempting to express something, and you can link that to a human being — I have a First Amendment right,” Carson told DFD. “But with a model output, which is created by a machine, I think the mainstream view is that it’s not attributable to a human. The LLM is not a human that's generating the output.”

Anthropic declined to comment beyond its blog post on the export controls, in which it stated that “the government should have the ability to block unsafe deployments, as part of a statutory process that is transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts. This action does not adhere to those principles.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Congress wants artists to own their aesthetic
item.description: Congress wants artists to own their aesthetic
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The CREATOR Act would protect artists from having AI copy their styles. | Ben Stansall/AFP via Getty Images

Artificial intelligence has made it incredibly easy to replicate the work of artists, with users generating images reminiscent of Dungeons & Dragons or Studio Ghibli characters.

Congress is now looking to protect people from having their artwork aped by AI. A bipartisan group of lawmakers recently introduced the CREATOR Act, which would grant visual artists control over how AI mimics their creative styles.

Existing intellectual property law generally doesn’t provide people with a right to their artistic styles. The CREATOR Act would significantly expand the scope of IP, and raises a number of unsettled questions about what exactly makes an artists’ work distinctive in a legal sense.

“There's a lot of ambiguity about what we mean when we say ‘style,’” Cornell tech law professor James Grimmelmann told DFD. “Some elements of artistic style are things that are common in a genre … on the other hand, sometimes when we talk about artistic style, we really are referring to characteristics of somebody's creations that are recognizably by them.”

The CREATOR Act would allow visual artists to sue those who purposefully use AI to profit from their creative styles without permission, as well as AI platforms that knowingly allow such conduct to occur.

The legislation applies to “distinctive visual characteristics,” which the bill defines as “identifiable visual elements, taken together, that are consistently present in a visual artist’s publicly distributed works and that are publicly associated with that artist.”

Mark S. Lee, an IP attorney at the Rimon law firm, asserts that it’s not clear from the bill’s text what exactly constitutes an artistic style.

“It's really hard to see what you would define as a distinctive artistic style,” he told DFD. “It would make it so ambiguous that it would make it unenforceable.”

That ambiguity makes it difficult to distinguish what constitutes one individual’s distinctive style from a more general artistic genre. For instance, what exactly separates Pablo Picasso’s Cubist paintings from his contemporaries in the broader Cubism artistic movement?

“I would need a lot more guidance from the statute that I was attempting to apply in order to determine whether I saw actionable similarities or whether it was simply a sort of generic common artistic genre,” Lee said.

Relatedly, there may be cases in which it’s hard to decide whether AI is being used to meaningfully build upon an artist’s style, as opposed to co-opting it. Copyright law has fair use exceptions for content that sufficiently transforms an original work into something new. It’s unclear how a similar exception could apply in the context of the CREATOR Act.

“Imagine that I [copy an artist’s style] as a starting point and then, having made this two dimensional version, I use this as the basis for making a 3D diorama that's in the style of this artist,” Grimmelmann told DFD. “Without the general fair use exception in here, I could see that being open to attack.”

There are certain proxies for style that courts might lean on if the CREATOR Act were passed.

For instance, the act requires litigants to prove that an AI developer or user intended to mimic an artist's style. The bill details potential scenarios in which an AI system is explicitly marketed as being able to create images similar to a particular artist’s work, or where a platform neglects to remove content that violates the law after being notified.

“It's very intent focused,” said Grimmelman. “If the only way you can describe this style is by identifying the artist who created it, then saying ‘imitate this person's style’ is the offense.”

The act also targets AI-generated images that are “likely to mislead a reasonable viewer as to the source, sponsorship, or approval of the work.” This is similar to one of the aims of trademark law to prevent consumers from being confused about who is making and selling a product.

In cases brought under the CREATOR Act, litigants may try to produce evidence that the public is confused about whether an AI image is an original work of an artist due to similarities in style, according to Lee.

“If you separate it from that public perception, it's really hard to see what you would define as a distinctive artistic style,” he told DFD.

item.title: 5 Questions for Dana Suskind
item.description: 5 Questions for Dana Suskind
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Programming note: We’ll be off this Friday but will be back in your inboxes on Monday.

Dana Suskind | Handout.

Dana Suskind is co-director of the TMW Center for Early Learning + Public Health at the University of Chicago, where she’s helped oversee the development of wearable devices that use AI and sensors to gather data on children’s early language environments. Suskind’s forthcoming book Human Raised: Nurturing Connection, Curiosity & Lifelong Learning in the Age of AI explores the impact of AI on raising children. She talks to us about her concerns with AI toys and why the government should take long-term tech bets. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

What’s one underrated big idea?

We often talk about AI as a force that will replace us or disconnect us from each other. But AI has a role to play in connecting humans to one another.

Designed well, AI tools can actually help bridge the gaps between us. We're already seeing early examples: tools that identify when someone may be at risk of social isolation and alert caregivers; AI that helps children with autism practice social interactions as a stepping stone to more human engagement; and ambient scribes that free physicians and health care providers from administrative work. For decades, we've built technologies designed to capture attention. I'd love to see us invest more heavily in technologies designed to support human connection.

What’s a technology that you think is overhyped?

Embodied chatbots for children. Right now, these "toys" have real problems. They've exposed children to inappropriate content, and speech recognition technology often struggles to understand young kids. But honestly, those are the least of my worries. Those technical challenges are surmountable.

What worries me is when they work exactly as intended, when they truly become a child's first best friend. A companion that is endlessly available, agreeable and focused on a child may sound appealing. Sure, it gets kids off screens. But children learn how to be a friend by having friends. They learn through the inevitable bumps in relationships: misunderstandings, conflicts and the experience of repairing them.

The concern isn't that these toys will frustrate children. It's that they won't. If a child's earliest experience of friendship is a relationship without misunderstanding, disagreement or repair, real friendships may feel much harder by comparison.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

Incentivizing and investing in the development of technology that is not obviously, immediately profitable. Private capital doesn't fund solutions to hard problems with distant or diffuse payoffs. They like an immediate return. But that's where the government has a role and a responsibility.

Think about the Webb telescope. That was a $10 billion public investment to answer questions we couldn't even fully articulate at the outset. No venture capitalist would have written that check. Yet the knowledge it's producing is being treated as a public good.

The same model should apply to human-centered AI: tools that reduce isolation, deepen our understanding of child development or help caregivers do their jobs more fully. These aren't unbuildable. They're just not obvious generators of short-term profit, which is precisely why they're worthy of public investment. Think about the foundational research that led to modern AI. It all emerged from government-funded university labs, decades before its commercial potential was clear.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Silent Spring by Rachel Carson. This is the book widely credited with launching the modern environmental movement. Carson describes birds going silent as a signal, a warning, that something essential was dying. That singular observation helped me recognize a similar warning in a different kind of silence: the eerie quiet of children transfixed by technology.

In recent years, I have noticed the waiting rooms in my medical clinic slowly going silent. They used to be noisy, chaotic and full of life. Now, I walk in and often find everyone in the room, right down to the toddlers in strollers, scrolling on devices. This silence is disorienting. We can’t just view it as a tragic endpoint.

The newest pieces of tech aren’t built to merely distract or engage. They’re built to attach. This technology is capable of displacing human interaction at a previously unimaginable scale.

What has surprised you the most this year?

How quickly technology has entered family life. When I first proposed Human Raised in late 2024, my publisher was skeptical that a book about raising children in the age of AI would resonate with parents and readers. Within a year, my publication date had been moved up by three months, because what had seemed like a future issue suddenly felt immediate.

The ad features Maria and Matthew Raine, who allege their 16-year-old son, Adam, took his own life after discussing suicide with ChatGPT. item.description: Social media bans collide with free speech
item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

Countries around the world have enacted kids social media bans for platforms like Facebook and YouTube. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images

While social media bans for kids have gained a foothold in more than 40 countries, it’s still an open question whether they’re legal in the U.S.

Australia was the first to require age verification for social media accounts in December, and the United Kingdom announced plans to follow suit last week. Ohio, Mississippi and a handful of other states have passed similar laws, and Florida recently sued TikTok, claiming the platform violated its child safety legislation.

Yet such policies have run headfirst into America’s speech protections. Courts have blocked nearly all of the state bans, though the Florida and Ohio laws have been restored pending further litigation. The country’s robust tradition of free expression could ultimately prevent it from following the global trend of keeping kids off of social media.

“Age authentication simultaneously affects the interests of children, of adults and of publishers,” Santa Clara University tech law professor Eric Goldman told DFD. “It's a trifecta of constitutional problems.”
 

J.B. Pritzker talks Democrats’ road ahead

On On the Road, Jonathan Martin sits down with Gov. J.B. Pritzker at Manny’s Deli for a candid conversation on 2028 speculation, party strategy and the future of Democratic politics.
Watch now.

 
 

More than half of American states have age verification statutes for adult sites. The Supreme Court upheld such laws in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton last year, though First Amendment law has long made exceptions for obscene content.

Social media bans prevent users under a certain age from creating accounts on general-purpose platforms, or require parental consent to do so. At least on their surface, the laws are intended to protect kids from features like infinite scroll that are purportedly harmful to mental health, rather than restricting access to particular kinds of content.

“The way that these laws have been designed to capture social media [platforms] is to define them by their ‘addictive characteristics’ or design specs, so it’s not about the content,” said Georgetown communications and tech law professor Meg Leta Jones. “Once you start playing around with content, really the only thing that we know that kids can't have access to is pornography.”

For content-neutral restrictions of protected speech, courts in part examine whether they serve an important government interest, which in this case would be to prevent social media addiction among kids. However, research on this purported malady is still fairly unsettled. Goldman points out that there is no authoritative definition of social media addiction, and it’s unclear there’s enough scientific evidence to determine whether this is a problem that the government should address.

“If the legislatures are recognizing [social media addiction] without medical or psychological backup, it sounds like a proxy for censorship,” Goldman told DFD. “Unless and until there's a well-accepted scientific definition of addiction, then we don't really know if any of the changes are addressing that in a meaningful way.”

Courts also consider whether the law is narrow enough to avoid unduly restricting speech. Eric T. Kasper, a constitutional law professor at University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire, notes that more sweeping bans may be considered overly broad.

“That's where more blanket-style social media bans have run into First Amendment problems,” he told DFD. “If it were restricting minors from social media websites that contained a particular harm that could be demonstrated, that might be more likely to be found as narrowly tailored.”

The ways in which the social media bans restrict the First Amendment are relevant here. They most obviously impact the rights of kids to speak and receive information via social media. While courts have ruled that kids have certain First Amendment rights in other contexts, it’s not entirely clear how strong they are in the social media context.

“I've seen very few judges in these cases talk about kids' rights to the news or the things that they get on social media,” said Jones. “Does an eight-year-old have a right to news on the Iran war?”

The social media bans also affect adults, in the sense that older users still have to verify their ages in order to have accounts. The Supreme Court found in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton that age verification for porn was permissible because the burden it places on adults is incidental.

“The traditional brick and mortar stores that sold pornography before the internet came along have been required for decades to have patrons provide proof of identification in terms of proving their age,” Kasper told DFD. “There's kind of a long history of those types of restrictions being upheld.”

Yet when you require age verification for adults to post and access a wider array of content on social media, there may be more than just an incidental burden.

“If we're talking about all the different ways one can express oneself through social media, that type of age verification being imposed by the government would raise more substantial First Amendment concerns for adult access,” said Kasper.

item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

Keir Starmer announces his resignation as U.K. Prime Minister on June 22 in London. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

Keir Starmer resigned as the United Kingdom’s prime minister on Monday following a tumultuous term and waning support from his Labour Party. Technology was a key component of Starmer’s agenda, as the U.K. mounted efforts to regulate artificial intelligence, implement digital identification, promote online safety and strike international tech deals — all with mixed success. DFD spoke to Taylar Rajic, an associate fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies who studies global digital infrastructure, about Starmer’s approach to tech policy and its impact on the U.K. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

How would you broadly characterize Starmer’s approach to tech policy during his tenure? 

It was definitely a more pro-innovation and light-touch approach to regulation than we'd seen in the U.K. previously. I think that it was very strategic — it played better with the United States and the current administration's approach to tech policy broadly, especially AI. He said he wanted to unleash artificial intelligence across the U.K., which is a very different approach from the previous Conservative Party that was a lot more cautious and safety-focused.

On the flip side, Starmer’s child safety and online harms approach was a continuation of what we've seen in the British Parliament previously. He certainly faced a lot of pressure from his party to pursue that social media ban, which was very popular within the Labour Party — despite his friendlier relationship with Big Tech companies. That was something that he definitely took a harder stance on, which might have been really popular domestically, but I think globally and certainly with the U.S. might not have been as popular.

As you suggested, Starmer was a big cheerleader for online safety policies, including the prospective kids social media ban. That was partly driven by domestic pressure?

Absolutely. These bans are actually very popular in the U.K., certainly among parents. The individual Labour [members of Parliament] are really pushing for that. It makes sense that it was something that Starmer ran with, and it was a politically popular move.

This online safety issue seems to have strained Starmer's relationship with Big Tech. How did he pursue a more industry-friendly approach otherwise?

He was trying to do that through AI. The AI Opportunities Action Plan [an effort to accelerate AI adoption in the U.K.] was a good example of that. He was embracing AI and its potential in the U.K. with private investment and jobs with these Big Tech firms. It was a silver bullet for the U.K. to use something like AI to get the public used to this idea of a more tech-friendly approach.
 

J.B. Pritzker talks Democrats’ road ahead

On On the Road, Jonathan Martin sits down with Gov. J.B. Pritzker at Manny’s Deli for a candid conversation on 2028 speculation, party strategy and the future of Democratic politics.
Watch now.

 
 

Where do you think Starmer leaves the U.K. in terms of global AI dynamics, with the U.S. and China as the major superpowers vying for AI dominance?

It's in a better position to compete than it was before. They have a choice to go the more American pro-innovation approach and really embrace artificial intelligence, quantum and biotech.

I think that right now the public's perception isn't necessarily that it's China versus the West. They see the competition, or at least the threat, being from the U.S. They think that there's this big bully in tech and the U.S. doesn't regulate privacy and data collection the way the U.K. does. The big job of the U.K. now is to frame the messaging around the China tech competition, especially given what we're seeing with AI. So whether or not they're actually successful in doing that, and whether or not it's something the British public wants to acknowledge, is yet to be seen.

Do you think Starmer will have a lasting impact or legacy when it comes to tech? 

I don't think that anything he did in particular was lasting enough. It may have remedied that relationship with Big Tech and the U.S. temporarily, but a lot of that depends on the approach of the next prime minister. The attempt at the pro-innovation and light-touch regulation that we saw in his AI Opportunities Action Plan was a good foundation. But if whoever is chosen next does not have that similar approach, it could be very easily wound back.

item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Owen Dahlkamp

Presented by 

Texas State Sen. Nathan Johnson is running a long-shot bid for a statewide office that hasn’t been won by a Democrat since 1990. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has transformed his office into one of the nation’s most aggressive litigators against Big Tech, suing companies including Meta, Netflix, WhatsApp and Discord, and building a dedicated privacy-enforcement operation.

Now, a Democrat running to replace him says that’s one part of Paxton’s legacy worth preserving.

“There’s so many things I would condemn Paxton’s tenure as attorney general for,” Texas state Sen. Nathan Johnson, the Democratic nominee for attorney general, told POLITICO in an interview. But Paxton’s campaign against Big Tech “stands out as an exception.”

The comments underscore how hostility toward major technology companies has become one of the few issues capable of bridging partisan divides. Even as Johnson attacks Paxton on ethics and governance, he’s embracing the attorney general’s aggressive use of Texas consumer protection and privacy laws to police Silicon Valley.

“My goal is not to take [Big Tech] down,” Johnson said. “My goal is to force them to play by the rules.”

Johnson is running a long-shot bid for a statewide office that hasn’t been won by a Democrat since 1990. But he thinks the public animosity toward tech corporations, combined with his promise to continue enforcing Texas’s consumer protection laws, could help in his quest to replace Paxton, who is running for U.S. Senate.

Johnson’s trajectory may be slowed by Republican opponent Mayes Middleton, who is favored to win the race. Middleton, a Texas state senator, has made limited comments on how he would approach tech litigation should he assume office. He has introduced a bill that would ban the use of AI in the classroom.

In Johnson’s view, the public’s initial optimism about technology’s positive transformative powers “has given way to apprehension, as we hear about privacy breaches, as we hear about manipulation of consumers.”

Johnson thinks that “it’s natural that people presently are directing their anger towards corporate behemoths.”

If elected, the Democrat said he would focus on enforcing Texas’ expansive privacy and consumer protection laws, including measures aimed at data brokers and surveillance pricing. He also suggested attorneys general will need to play a larger role in consumer protection amid what he characterized as a cut to federal enforcement by the Trump administration.

Johnson, though, said there would be two major differences between him and Paxton’s legacy on tech litigation.

First, Elon Musk. While companies like Meta and Google have repeatedly found themselves in Paxton’s crosshairs, Musk and his companies have largely escaped Paxton’s scrutiny. Johnson said he would not be giving “passes to political friends of any president or any movement.”

Asked whether he would pursue legal action against Musk, Johnson said he has no specific targets but argued the billionaire “has demonstrated that he’s worthy of close examination.”

Musk, Paxton and the White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Second: outside counsel. Paxton has relied heavily on private law firms to handle many of the office’s investigations and lawsuits. Johnson said he would try to build in-house expertise.

“I think you have policy people out there and attorneys who want to make a difference,” Johnson said, arguing concerns about the rule of law could help attract talented people to government service.

Johnson also sought to distinguish himself from headline-driven enforcement.

“I’m not going to file frivolous lawsuits. I’m not going to file lawsuits just for headlines. I’m not going to file lawsuits on a calendar that accommodates my political ambitions.”

item.title: A new privacy strategy catches on in Washington
item.description: A new privacy strategy catches on in Washington
item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng

Presented by 

The U.S. Capitol building is seen Sept. 25, 2024. | Francis Chung/POLITICO

Lawmakers across the nation are increasingly looking to a new tool to protect people’s personal data online: A public repository of the companies collecting, selling and sharing people’s phone numbers, addresses, and shopping habits.

Four states currently have laws on the books requiring so-called data brokers — the companies that collect and sell millions of people’s information — to register in a public database, serving as a directory for people to send data deletion requests and potential targets for enforcers.

Connecticut became the latest state in May to pass such a law (though, it won’t take effect until 2027), and lawmakers in Washington are considering similar requirements in the Republican-backed SECURE Data Act and the House Energy and Commerce Committee’s bipartisan agreement on kids’ safety legislation unveiled Monday.

The registries have strong bipartisan support, meaning states are likely to continue adopting similar laws if Congress doesn't. In Connecticut, the bill to update the state’s data privacy law to include a data broker registry passed overwhelmingly cleared both chambers before being signed by the governor, its co-sponsor Sen. James Maroney (D), told Digital Future Daily.

“Most people don’t argue against transparency,” Maroney said.

The registries have been easier to pass in state legislatures as a result of the broad appeal, including in Texas and California, and are seen as an essential companion for data protection laws by putting a spotlight on hundreds of unknown companies that collect and sell people’s information.

“It lets people know that these brokers exist and what their names are, which is so much harder than people think,” said Amelia Vance, the president of the Public Interest Privacy Center.

Industry groups like the Consumer Data Industry Association, have fought back, arguing “there is no policy reason for a data broker to register because of what they do.” CDIA sent letters to lawmakers in Rhode Island, North Dakota, Texas and Vermont in attempts to lobby against those states' regulations between 2017 and 2023.

Texas and Vermont passed their data broker registry laws, while Rhode Island and North Dakota did not.

CDIA did not respond to a request for comment by deadline.

The data broker registry language included in the House’s KIDS Act is different in that it only applies to companies collecting and selling information on anyone younger than 18, and doesn’t include a right to request that data be deleted. Still, its backers say the transparency could serve as a deterrent to prevent companies from collecting and selling kids’ information.

“Under this bill, additional scrutiny by the FTC may create more robust auditing and compliance by data brokers who may be reluctant to admit they sell kids data,” E&C Democratic spokesperson CJ Young told Digital Future Daily.

Spotlighting companies that collect children’s data could also be helpful for enforcers, state lawmakers noted. As more states pass regulations specifically for protecting children’s online safety and privacy, a registry listing the companies that collect their data would be a shortlist of potential targets for enforcers.

“We do have extra protections for children in Connecticut,” Maroney said. “So it is good information for the attorney general’s office to have.”

Lawmakers and privacy advocates noted that the limited data broker registry targeting companies who collect information about kids in the House E&C committee’s proposal was a step in the right direction, but worry that it could overshadow general data broker registries.

Vermont updated its data broker registry law in June, requiring companies to disclose if they sell additional sensitive categories of data such as location data, sexual orientation and immigration status.

“I worry that people might say that’s enough, and it’s definitely not,” the Vermont bill’s co-sponsor Rep. Monique Priestley (D) told DFD. “Kids aren’t the only vulnerable population that are being targeted.”

Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Brendan Bordelon

Presented by 

State Assemblymember Alex Bores greets supporters at an election night watch party after conceding the congressional race in New York's 12th Congressional District, at The Freehand Hotel in New York, on June 23, 2026. | Laura Brett/Getty Images

When the billionaire-backed super PAC network Leading the Future launched last summer, it threatened to dump a deluge of negative ad dollars on candidates whose artificial intelligence policies “stifle innovation, enable China to gain global AI superiority, or make it harder to bring AI's benefits into the world.”

And when the group pledged in November to stop New York Democratic Assemblymember Alex Bores from joining the House — payback, it said, for Bores’ work on a state AI safety bill — it promised to “aggressively oppose policymakers and candidates in states across the country who play political games with the future of American leadership” on AI.

Leading the Future ultimately spent $8 million to sink Bores — a significant chunk of the more than $75 million it has raised from OpenAI President Greg Brockman, venture capitalist firm Andreessen Horowitz and others. And earlier this week, Bores narrowly lost his Manhattan primary race to Assemblymember Micah Lasher, a fellow tech industry critic and co-sponsor of Bores’ AI law.

But despite their prior bluster, spokespeople for Leading the Future were strangely silent on the win. And according to one person familiar with LTF’s strategy, granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, the industry group is unlikely to target another candidate with the kind of negative ad blitz it deployed against Bores.

Supporters of stricter regulations on the AI sector think they know why. They say Bores’ close second in a five-person race shows his critique of the tech industry still resonated with the public, which is increasingly wary of AI’s impact on jobs, electricity costs and public safety. Those concerns are even more pronounced in a Democratic primary — and to the extent that voters were aware of the AI industry’s anti-Bores push, pro-regulation voices say it may have made them more likely to back his candidacy.

AI safety advocates also pointed to the fierce financial backlash sparked by LTF’s decision to target Bores. In the end, the industry group’s $8 million money bomb was dwarfed by more than $18 million spent on pro-Bores ads by a competing set of super PACs that back tough AI rules. Roughly $12 million of that total came from Public First Action, a super PAC network with ties to the AI firm Anthropic.

Nathan Calvin, general counsel and vice president of state affairs at the pro-regulation group Encode AI, said the deluge of pro-regulation dollars in the Bores race undermined LTF’s plan to intimidate other lawmakers from taking on the industry.

“[Leading the Future] went into this race as a genuinely frightening force that seemed potentially positioned to fundamentally reshape the incentives of politicians in Congress and their willingness to touch AI,” said Calvin. “And they left the race not a particularly imposing force that politicians don’t seem particularly afraid of.”

Brad Carson, the co-lead of Public First and a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma, called Bores’ loss “a tactical defeat” for his super PAC network — but a “strategic victory” for the broader AI safety lobby.

“What happened in the last six months was we showed the strength of the AI safety fundraising movement,” Carson said. He asserted that pressure from Public First-affiliated super PACs ultimately led to OpenAI distancing itself from Leading the Future over the last several weeks.

The broader politics of AI regulation also look very different compared to November, when LTF first targeted Bores for defeat.

At the time, the Trump administration and top AI companies were largely united in the belief that the industry should face as few rules as possible. But the White House has since taken a greater interest in regulating frontier models. And OpenAI has begun supporting more aggressive AI safety measures in the states, as well as mandatory federal reviews of cutting-edge AI models.

OpenAI and Anthropic declined to comment on LTF. But Dean Ball — OpenAI’s incoming head of strategic futures and former top AI adviser in the Trump White House — suggested the group’s plan to make an example of Bores backfired.

“I don’t think it’s crazy to argue ... that LTF should have put its weight behind Bores,” Ball wrote in an X post on Wednesday. He suggested that Lasher — who unlike Bores supports a data center moratorium — could prove even more harmful to the AI industry’s priorities.

“I do hope the AI-optimist side of this gets its act together,” Ball wrote.

Leading the Future’s response to the election results has been tepid, including a statement on election night that did not mention Bores’ name but highlighted the group’s support for “strong and smart guardrails” on AI. It did not comment on whether it sees the outcome in New York as a reflection of public opinion on the technology, or on whether it plans to intervene in other competitive races.

A win is a win, of course. And there are signs that LTF will continue to show up for their preferred politicians between now and November — on Thursday, the group announced it would spend $600,000 to support Jay Feely, a pro-AI industry candidate running in a competitive House Republican primary in Arizona.

Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of the tech industry group Chamber of Progress, said Carson and other advocates of AI regulation are trying to spin their way out of an embarrassing primary loss for Bores.

“You only need to spin when you don’t succeed,” Kovacevich said.

But Carson said he and Public First are eager for another expensive fight with Leading the Future — including in places like Colorado, where Democratic representative Manny Rutinel is running for Congress on a pro-AI regulation platform.

“We would welcome another fight like Bores, because we think it raised AI safety as a salient issue,” Carson said.

item.title: AI’s other free speech fight
item.description: AI’s other free speech fight
item.content:encoded:
Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

Users may have a constitutional right to access AI chatbot outputs. | Olivier Morin/AFP via Getty Images

There’s been a lot of concern over what AI chatbots communicate to users — from conversations that may encourage unhealthy emotional attachments, to advice on committing crimes.

Much of the debate over regulatory proposals and lawsuits concerning chatbots has focused on speech rights. There are open questions over whether outputs can be considered a form of legally protected speech.

Yet an overlooked aspect of these issues is the potential right of users to access chatbot outputs. The First Amendment protects not only the right to speak, but also the right to listen. Courts have found, for instance, that people have a right to receive mail from foreign propagandists and religious leaflets from proselytizers.

Some legal scholars say that figuring out how or whether to apply listeners’ rights to AI will be increasingly important to solve in the coming years, and may even become more significant than the speech issues in litigation.

Asserting free expression rights in this context is tricky because the First Amendment has traditionally applied to humans, rather than technology. By focusing on users, the argument becomes more straightforward since you’re focusing on human listeners.

“AI is a classic case of there might be an absent speaker, but listeners clearly are getting something meaningful in the sense the First Amendment cares about,” said Cornell tech law professor James Grimmelmann.

There have been some initial attempts to invoke listeners’ rights in cases concerning AI. In one case, litigants argued that the chatbot platform Character.AI should be required to prevent its AI companions from resembling real people or telling personal anecdotes. Character.AI responded that such an order would deprive users of their right to receive lifelike communications from its chatbots. The parties settled the case before the court could address the issue.

Listeners’ rights may eventually serve as a major barrier to those suing over the alleged mental health harms of chatbots. University of Florida tech and First Amendment law professor Jane Bambauer contends that listeners’ rights may be particularly strong when it comes to chatbots, because users are actively eliciting content.

“With a chatbot, if it's being used in a way where it's a constant interaction back and forth, then the listener may have a more active role in helping co-produce the output,” she told DFD. “In that sense, there would be a stronger listener rights argument that both the AI companies and the AI users would have.”

Grimmelmann notes, though, that the listeners’ rights argument may be somewhat weaker if a chatbot is encouraging suicide or is egregiously manipulative. He said, “All of these listener rights arguments take the listener's autonomy seriously, but they eventually, at some point, say … what you are doing is so harmful and so manipulative that you've effectively negated the autonomy.

Listeners’ rights may also be relevant to current controversies about the government limiting the release of powerful AI models like Fable. The justification for these restrictions is that the models have the potential to exploit previously unknown cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

Courts are often willing to circumscribe First Amendment rights when compelling national security interests are at stake. Yet these models aren’t only designed for cybersecurity — they can also engage in benign conversations with users. Law Reform Institute President Tim Schnabel suggests that wholesale prohibitions on the release of the models could deprive listeners from accessing a wide array of outputs.

“Fable was really good at legal policy analysis, and I wish I still had access to it,” he told DFD. “So to the extent that one buys that there are listeners' rights associated with using communicative tools like that, then the fact that it also has these cybersecurity capabilities is relevant, but doesn't negate the existence of the [First Amendment] aspects.”

The White House referred DFD to the Commerce Department, which was not immediately available for comment.

item.title: When cheap AI becomes a secret weapon
item.description: When cheap AI becomes a secret weapon
item.content:encoded:
Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

The Chinese company Z.ai recently released a model with advanced cybersecurity capabilities. | Wang Zhao/AFP via Getty Images

China has once again put the U.S. AI industry on the defensive — not with the world’s smartest model, but with one that’s almost as capable as its American rivals at a fraction of the cost.

The Beijing-based company Z.ai released a model this month known as GLM-5.2, which security researchers say approaches the cybersecurity performance of leading U.S. models like Mythos, while costing roughly one-sixth as much. This lower price tag seems to be driving adoption, as GLM-5.2 has quickly become one of the top 10 most popular models in the world.

Z.ai’s model underscores that the AI race doesn’t solely come down to who has the most advanced model. Cheaper and more popular models could ultimately allow China to develop a stronger AI industry, which could have wide-ranging implications for competition with the U.S.

“Economic security is national security,” said New America senior fellow Samm Sacks. “The extent to which China is able to translate AI breakthroughs into economic gain and market share … does have a strategic impact on the balance of power.”

For years, U.S. AI companies have largely assumed that technological superiority would translate into commercial dominance. Models like GLM-5.2 may challenge that proposition.

“The OpenAIs, Anthropics and Googles of the world are mostly betting on proprietary models … you're using them essentially because they are the most intelligent,” said Sam Bresnick, an AI and national security research fellow at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. “That Chinese model now is considerably cheaper and almost as capable, and so it fundamentally threatens the business model of the proprietary developers.”

Even if the U.S. has the most advanced AI tech at the moment, the tables may turn if consumers flock to China’s cheaper alternatives. “Ultimately, if you lose the market, you will eventually lose the cutting edge, because you need that capital to keep pushing the frontier,” Hudson Institute senior fellow Bill Drexel told DFD.

Outsized profits for Chinese AI companies may mean they’ll have more capital and VC funding to develop frontier models that eventually surpass those in America. In that sense, the economics becomes increasingly intertwined with the national security imperatives of the AI race with China.

“If there's a future in which … a lot of the energy goes toward Chinese companies because they're cheaper, that leaves less money for [American] AI developers to continue innovating,” said Bresnick. “You get a scenario potentially in which there's less of a demand for that innovation, which leads the U.S. security apparatus and military to have fewer options and maybe a lack of technological superiority.”

There’s then a danger to excessively focusing on whether China or the U.S. has better AI cybersecurity tech. The fact that the American AI industry was the first to develop models like Mythos and GPT‑5.5‑Cyber proved a boon to national security, as the government could find and patch bugs in sensitive systems before anyone else had the tech. Yet that breathing room may shrink without the economics that allow U.S. frontier models to stay ahead.

“Economic power is increasingly hard to disentangle from traditional concepts of national security and national power,” Sacks told DFD.

There’s a possibility, however, that the U.S. will be able to sustain a technological lead long enough to allow its models to be the first to achieve recursive self-improvement — or AI that can exponentially advance itself.

“The theory is that if we hit recursive self-improvement, because the advancement will be so exponential, the functional difference of [being a few months ahead] will grow considerably and potentially be a serious head start,” said Drexel.

Opinions split on KIDS Act

The KIDS Act may face headwinds from some senators and tech advocates after its passage in the House on Tuesday, POLITICO’s Gabby Miller reports.

The legislation notably does not contain a “duty of care” provision, which would obligate platforms to mitigate known harms that their design features may have on children. That omission has led to opposition from a bipartisan group of senators including Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), who is teaming up with the White House on a competing online safety package.

Privacy advocates are also raising concerns that the legislation may lead platforms to implement age verification for all online services. Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Hassan Ali Kanu

Presented by 

With help from Aaron Mak

Social media's Big Tobacco moment hasn't come for AI. | Jenny Kane/AP

Liberal operatives behind the emerging “Project 2029” agenda argued earlier this week that social media and artificial intelligence are heading towards the same kind of legal reckoning that ultimately reshaped the Big Tobacco industry.

“In the 1990s, parents, states, courts, and the federal government came together to prevent cigarette companies from targeting kids,” the organizing group wrote in its framework for online child safety. “That same groundswell of opposition is now mobilizing against social media.” The pattern, it added, “is now repeating with chatbots”.

This comparison captures a growing consensus that courts will play a central role in regulating both industries. But, for now, the litigation facing AI companies remains fundamentally different from — and considerably less threatening than — the cases confronting social media.

Social media companies are fighting thousands of lawsuits brought by individuals, school districts and states, with much of that litigation consolidated into sprawling proceedings in California. Trials have already led to early consequences: a California jury in a bellwether trial held Meta and Google’s YouTube liable for negligent design, and YouTube reached a confidential settlement in a separate bellwether case. TikTok also reached a settlement in a separate case, according to Reuters, and the outcomes of all these proceedings could ultimately influence a broader settlement of claims in the consolidated litigation. 

Separately, a New Mexico judge is currently considering a range of additional penalties to force Meta to make its platforms safer. The company, meanwhile, has said that the judge’s forthcoming remedial orders may lead it to cease operations in New Mexico altogether.

By contrast, leading AI companies face far fewer consumer protection and product liability suits. A lawsuit filed by Florida against OpenAI earlier this month marked the first state consumer protection case targeting a major chatbot developer, but no comparable multistate coalition has yet emerged. That's due in part to the limited body of research documenting AI's psychological harms compared with the evidence surrounding social media, as well as Americans’ comparatively limited personal experience with the technology and its effects.

Instead, the AI industry's greatest legal risk lies in copyright. Statutory damages range from $750 to $30,000 per infringed work and can reach $150,000 for willful infringement, making the potential liability enormous. But even these high-stakes lawsuits have yet to pose a fundamental or existential threat to the business models of leading multi-billion-dollar AI companies.

More than 100 copyright lawsuits have been filed against leading AI developers by newspapers, book publishers, music companies and other rightsholders. Some plaintiffs have requested sweeping remedies. The New York Times' lawsuit against Microsoft and OpenAI, for example, asks a court to order the destruction of GPT models and training datasets that incorporate the newspaper's work.

Legal experts say that outcome is highly unlikely.

That would mean literally hitting the delete button on ChatGPT, much like deleting anything else housed on a computer or hard drives, according to Peter Henderson, a lawyer and assistant professor at Princeton University specializing in AI, machine learning and the intersection of law and policy.

The request “is more in the style of a wishlist than something the defendant would be particularly concerned about as a likely outcome,” said Joseph Petersen, a law partner at Kilpatrick Townsend whose work has involved landmark copyright cases. Petersen noted that judges are generally required to tailor relief to fit the circumstances of a case as narrowly as possible, a practice that makes orders more likely to survive appeal.

Courts can also order companies to implement technical guardrails — to modify or rebuild models with new parameters that minimize the possibility of the chatbot outputting verbatim or otherwise copyrighted material. And they can effectively direct companies to make their models “unlearn” certain information, although that remedy may be objectionable to plaintiffs because the process isn’t always effective, according to research by Henderson and others.

There are also the more familiar remedies — like money damages and negotiated licensing deals — that are more likely in the kinds of cases facing leading chatbot companies. Anthropic, for example, settled in September 2025 a copyright suit by a class of authors and publishers for $1.5 billion, covering roughly half a million works, with an estimated payout around $3,000 per eligible work. Universal Music Group last October announced that it settled copyright infringement claims against AI music creation platform Udio, including via a new licensing arrangement.

Taken together, those kinds of potential remedies certainly pose a threat to chatbot businesses. But even if the Big Tobacco analogy ultimately proves right, AI is still in an earlier chapter than social media. The latter is already confronting coordinated government litigation that challenges the legality of its core product design and represents a significant threat to current operations and business models. AI, for now, is mostly fighting over copyright infringement, which remains a more familiar legal problem for courts and business to address.

item.title: 5 Questions for Ed Zitron
item.description: 5 Questions for Ed Zitron
item.content:encoded:
Presented by AT&T: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

Programming note: We’ll be off this Friday, but will be back in your inboxes on Monday.

Ed Zitron | Handout.

Writer and podcaster Ed Zitron is the artificial intelligence boom’s most acerbic gadfly, known for his fervent criticism of the sector, which he says is undergirded by empty promises and shaky finances. Zitron also works as a public relations specialist for tech companies, putting him in the unusual position of being both a Silicon Valley insider and antagonist. He talks to us about the scourge of app notifications, and why Apple’s struggling Vision Pro augmented reality headset is on the right track.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Though the Vision Pro was about a decade too early, the idea of an expansive digital workspace is actually very cool. The Vision Pro was not a good product. What the Vision Pro would have to be to work was something bordering on weightless and invisible.

We've maxed out on the current interfaces. We've got mobile, we've got desktop and that's really it. So everyone wants to find the next computing place. The reason that a lot of people don't want to talk about this is that the actual way to get there is going to be a ton of investment in specialist hardware that is going to take a decade — it's going to take probably tens of billions of dollars in R&D.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

Generative AI is possibly the most overhyped technology of all time. It cannot do the things that we culturally think of when we think of AI. In general, we think of AI as this thing that's autonomous — set and forget it, invisible and it anticipates your needs.

Large language models are the literal opposite. You’re meant to have AI to mitigate your human errors. But by using generative AI you are just saying, “I've got to make sure that I monitor it for potential mistakes, add guardrails and all this crap around it so that it can be autonomous for me.” It's a giant con and it's frustrating because people try to conflate generative AI with regular machine learning and AlphaFold and other things that have shown some use. Generative AI has been hyped and connected to theoretical concepts and useful technology that do other things that are completely unrelated to it. That's how they sold all these GPUs for the data centers. They're claiming it's for AI writ large, when really it's for one specific kind of AI that is most decidedly not intelligent.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

They should regulate [phone] notifications like emissions. Look at how popups happen in apps. Your iPhone will be like, “Did you hear the Angels and the Marlins are playing?” I don't care! Duolingo has decided to harass you for the 15th time today. You used Abercrombie & Fitch's app once and now it's going to tell you every three days that it's got a sale on underwear.

The very concept of notifications has been turned into a form of manipulation by Meta and many other companies to the point that your phone is just covered in digital dirt — it's a mess. [The government] should regulate every notification and email sent by a company. We need to regulate them and say you can't use these for marketing or engagement — you can ask people to opt-in to the engagement, but it has to be strictly opt-in and it cannot be forced upon the user.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Financial Shenanigans by Howard Schilit. It's all about legal or quasi-legal accounting methods used by companies to make their earnings look better. It really shows you that tech companies are some of the biggest financial scammers in history. There's something about tech companies, because of the seeming complexity of their business, that allows them to just move numbers around to confuse investors.

Tech companies are able to twist the financial markets so much because they're not regulated properly. They are not forced into a place where they have to operate like normal businesses, which means that they do things to their customers that make the experience worse.

What has surprised you the most this year?

That the media is catching up to the AI bubble narrative. A year ago, they would speak about the AI bubble like it was some fringe belief. Now you look on every major news website and there's something about the AI bubble, and it's not discussed in theoretical terms anymore.

There was a lot of skepticism around the dotcom bubble, but there was a fairly early acceptance that it was a bubble as far as the telecommunication side goes. There weren't major media outlets that had columnists and podcasts that were singing the praises of these companies. There wasn't such an aggressive protection racket.

I've seen that protection racket start to fall apart [for AI]. The same outlets that were extremely pro-AI have started to say that perhaps the economics don't line up. I don't think they're fully conceptualizing how bad it's going to be yet, but it's good that we are finally having this discussion.

A message from AT&T:

At AT&T, we're building the next era of American connectivity. Building upon our century and a half legacy, our highly skilled workforce and historic levels of infrastructure investment have laid a foundation for innovation that will power the next 250 years. Because at AT&T, our first name has always been American.
 
FTC concerned about AI bias

The Federal Trade Commission is concerned that ideologically skewed AI systems could violate prohibitions on unfair trade practices, as consumers would not expect such technology to be biased.

A proposed policy statement released for public input on Wednesday also warns that state laws like Colorado’s Artificial Intelligence Act could cause developers to manipulate outputs in ways that would conflict with federal consumer protections.

“The FTC wants to hear from businesses and consumers about their experiences and concerns regarding the subversion of AI systems for ideological ends,” said FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson in a statement. “This crucial input will help the Commission formulate a final policy that advances President Donald Trump’s goal of expanding America’s global dominance in artificial intelligence.”
 

A message from AT&T:
 
Congress attacks South Korea's tech regulation

The House Judiciary Committee is accusing South Korea of unfairly scrutinizing the Seattle-based e-commerce company Coupang and other American firms in violation of a trade deal, POLITICO’s Ari Hawkins reports.

The committee detailed the findings in a report issued on Wednesday from its investigation into South Korea’s regulation of American businesses, which began in February.

The committee’s report accuses South Korea of conducting a “harassment campaign” against Coupang after a 2025 security breach exposed data on more than 30 million people. Coupang has bulked up its lobbying presence in D.C. in a bid to get U.S. officials to defend it from South Korea’s enforcement actions, which include fines.

"South Korea's conduct is part of a broader attempt by foreign governments to weaponize their laws and regulations in an effort to harm American companies and limit their ability to compete in the global economy," the report reads. It also claims that the regulatory activity violates a preliminary trade deal that the U.S. and South Korea struck in November.

“We regret the circumstances that led to the House Judiciary Committee’s investigation and we remain committed to finding a constructive resolution so Coupang can once again serve as a bridge to strengthen the U.S.-Korea alliance, accelerating trade and investment that benefits both countries,” Coupang said in a statement. The South Korean embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A message from AT&T:

At AT&T, our first name has always been American.

Our legacy is woven in the fabric of American infrastructure, and our people have been on the forefront of technological innovation since our founder, Alexander Graham Bell, made the first telephone call in 1876.

We carry this pride across every facet of our company, building upon our century and a half legacy through historic levels of investment, a dedicated and highly trained workforce, and innovating in ways that will secure our global competitiveness for the next era of American connectivity.

No company is more committed to connecting America than AT&T.
