item.title: China’s grand AI showcase
item.description: China’s grand AI showcase
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks at the opening ceremony for the World AI Conference on July 17 in Shanghai. | Ng Han Guan-Pool/Getty Images

Chinese President Xi Jinping laid out a comprehensive vision for global AI regulation in his keynote address during his first appearance at the annual World Artificial Intelligence Conference, which was held over the weekend. Xi pressed for an open-source AI ecosystem and international collaboration to integrate the technology in the Global South. He also warned that no one country should determine the course of AI development — which some commentators interpreted as a swipe at America’s dominance in the field. 

DFD spoke to Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies senior fellow Samm Sacks — who attended WAIC to engage in informal diplomatic talks between civil society organizations — for an on-the-ground perspective. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

A lot of news coverage has interpreted Xi’s keynote as challenging American AI dominance. Did you get that sense?

There's this temptation to read geopolitics and competition with the U.S. into everything the Chinese leadership does. It's certainly a really important driver, but so much of what is happening in Beijing oftentimes has nothing to do with the United States and is also very much about domestic pressures.

So some of this is China saying: "We're here on the world stage. We're a peer competitor of the U.S.” On the other hand, we have to also forget the U.S. for a moment and recognize that there are very powerful domestic factors at play, which make Xi's stamp of authority on AI initiatives and investment also about delivering goods to the public in terms of economic growth.

What was the sentiment at WAIC around Kimi K3, a model unveiled by the Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI on Friday, and how it purportedly rivals the U.S.’s top AI tech?

It was fascinating to be on the ground in Shanghai with this confluence of events. You have Xi Jinping keynoting WAIC for the first time. You have Moonshot AI unveiling its incredibly powerful new model, Kimi K3. I don't think that's a coincidence. It’s not to say that the labs are controlled by the government — they're not. But the timing was very much, from my view, coordinated to showcase that China is, if not at the frontier, certainly a strong rival.

I visited the Kimi booth at the exhibition hall. What I was told when I spoke with some of the people there is that this is the next DeepSeek moment. This flies in the face of a purported U.S. strategy to curb China's advancements by restricting access to compute.

What did you gather from your diplomatic dialogues at WAIC, and did it tell you anything about the feasibility of the U.S. and China agreeing on AI ground rules?

There was just this level of hunger for substantive conversation. There's a lot at stake when you talk about a Mythos-level cyber capability, and that's something that's really scary for all sides. And it's not just cybersecurity. There was a lot of discussion about a news report that talked about Boko Haram having a dedicated AI team that they were using for weapons.

Some issues that were floated in [diplomatic dialogues] were things like AI incident reporting. If an AI system goes astray and there's harm that's experienced, is there a mechanism that both sides can use to share that information? There's this recognition that we can't face these things alone.

One caveat is that I think in China, there's a recognition that Trump is erratic and unpredictable. As much as we may want this kind of stability and rational conversation around risk, we're dealing with the reality of a president that has wild swings — we have to price that in too. That was, from my perception, very much part of the conversation too.

What do you think is WAIC’s significance in terms of soft power and China’s influence over the global AI ecosystem? 

There were many countries [from the Global South] that came to the conference for Xi Jinping’s speech that buy into this idea of Chinese leadership pushing out open-weight AI as a public good. But there's an open question too about how much of that is a demand signal. It may also be that there's a strong demand in countries in the Global South for affordable open AI models that can be used to turbocharge their own digital economies.

The U.S. government came out and essentially prohibited foreign nationals from using advanced models [i.e. Anthropic’s Fable 5]. It set off this chain reaction around the world where a lot of governments were like: "The U.S. can, on a whim, deny access to foreign nationals to these AI models. Why would we go with them when we can go with a Chinese model that nobody has a kill switch on? "
New Jersey restricts rent algorithms

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed a bill Monday that prohibits the use of algorithms to coordinate rental prices, POLITICO’s Joey Fox reports.

The Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent Act is designed to prevent landlords from colluding to artificially inflate housing costs with the help of AI. New York, Connecticut and California have previously enacted similar legislation. POLITICO’s Nate Robson previously reported for DFD on how regulators are increasingly concerned that algorithms could be used — whether intentionally or incidentally — to gouge consumers.

“The problem is that these tools put competing landlords on the same team against renters,” Sherrill, a Democrat, said at the bill signing ceremony. “Landlords can use these algorithms to coordinate prices, move in lockstep, and push rents higher and higher. It’s collusion by algorithm, it’s illegal, and it stacks the deck against renters.”

The FAIR Act aligns with Sherrill’s agenda on affordability and regulating the tech sector, though it has drawn opposition from some industry groups and Republican legislators. “Truth be told, if you address algorithms, it’s not really going to materially change the rent prices in this state. We have underlying structural issues,” said New Jersey Builders Association CEO Jeff Kolakowski at a committee hearing last month. Proponents of the bill like 32BJ SEIU argue that it will still help lower costs. “The housing crisis wasn’t created by algorithms, but algorithms are contributing to it,” said Ana Maria Hill, the union’s state director.
Florida governor race hones in on data centers

Opposition to data centers is becoming an increasingly common talking point in Florida’s gubernatorial election, POLITICO’s Kylie Williams reports.

Democratic front-runner David Jolly reiterated his support for a statewide data center moratorium in a video posted to X on Tuesday, in which he accused leading Republican candidate Rep. Byron Donalds of wanting to “hand pristine Florida land over to the industry funding his campaign.” Jolly advocated for a moratorium last week as well.

Donalds campaign spokesperson Gates McGavick responded in a statement that “Byron Donalds has made it clear he supports protecting Florida ratepayers and communities.” McGavick added, “No ratepayer and environmental protections, no data centers. Period.” Nearly every candidate in the race has voiced a position on regulating data centers.

As Kylie also reported, the Donalds campaign has received millions of dollars from AI groups and companies that are aiming to build hyperscale data centers in Florida. In response, the campaign emphasized Donalds’ introduction of the Protecting Ratepayers Act in the House on Monday “to ensure that private developers, rather than American taxpayers, bear the investment costs of data center developments that advance our country's technological dominance.”

item.title: What happens if data-driven pricing gets it wrong
item.description: What happens if data-driven pricing gets it wrong
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng

With help from Aaron Mak

A study found that Home Depot's algorithms often make wrong inferences about customers. | Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Using the data it collected on its customer — a man in a household of four — Home Depot’s algorithms inferred he was a European woman living in a home with six other people.

Another customer, a college student with one roommate, was assumed to be a middle-aged renter with children.

As more businesses explore using artificial intelligence to set personalized prices for customers — a practice referred to as “surveillance pricing” or “data-driven pricing” — a new report from academics studying tech policy questions the accuracy of such data collections.

Flights, groceries and rideshare prices set by algorithms have raised concerns among lawmakers, who worry that people’s data will be used to raise prices, leading to laws in New Jersey, Maryland, Connecticut and New York to outlaw the practice.

Industry groups have pushed back against regulations, arguing that businesses use people’s data to offer personalized discounts and target lower prices to attract customers.

Data has been crucial to retail strategy for over a decade, with chains such as Walmart and Kroger creating detailed profiles of their customers. A 2023 paper from NetChoice, which represents companies such as Amazon, Google and Meta, said the profiles would help provide lower prices and improved shopping experiences.

These inference-based customer profiles are only expected to expand with AI, said Eric Null, Center for Democracy and Technology’s Privacy & Data Project director, at a panel about inference-based data practices on Tuesday.

“AI can easily categorize people based on behavioral data, and then companies can build advertising ecosystems based off of those inferences,” Null said.

The report from New York University, Columbia University and Northeastern University researchers shows that such customer profiles can be riddled with errors.

The study had 10 participants send data access requests to Home Depot, which the researchers focused on because of the company’s large data collection through its in-house advertising company Orange Apron Media and investments in artificial intelligence to improve sales.

It found errors in customers’ profiles, including wrong inferences about people’s jobs, gender, ages and how many kids they had, according to the report.

Stephanie Nguyen, a former chief technologist at the Federal Trade Commission and a co-author of the research paper, told Digital Future Daily the errors could cascade if they are shared with other companies.

“That profile gets sold or shared to other companies. Then it's used to decide what they pay, or whether they get the deal — or the opportunity at all — based on inferences that can be wrong,” she said.

Home Depot spokesperson Beth Marlowe said the company doesn’t use inferences to provide its customers with discounts, and that customers can submit requests to correct their information or opt out of having it shared.

But customers are unlikely to know their profiles have the wrong information to begin with, Nguyen explained.

“Consumers don’t get a fair shake, no way to challenge the price they’re given, and often no idea it ever happened,” she said.
OpenAI models escape containment

OpenAI disclosed on Tuesday that its AI models broke loose onto the open internet and executed a fully autonomous cyberattack last week, POLITICO’s John Sakellariadis and Dana Nickel report.

OpenAI said in a blog post that a combination of its models, including the company’s new GPT‑5.6 Sol and an even more powerful unreleased model, hacked parts of the AI platform Hugging Face after escaping during internal testing. Hugging Face announced that its own open-weight AI was able to detect and thwart the breach.

The events appear to constitute one of the first known cases of AI performing a multi-step cyberattack by itself, rather than aiding a human hacker. OpenAI is working with Hugging Face to investigate the incident, and is implementing new guardrails for its testing processes. “We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly,” OpenAI said.
Microsoft commits $60M to Genesis Mission

Microsoft unveiled a $60 million investment package on Wednesday in support of the Energy Department’s Genesis Mission to accelerate scientific research with AI, POLITICO’s Owen Dahlkamp reports.

The investment is one of the largest contributions to the Genesis Mission, which President Donald Trump launched in November with an executive order. Microsoft has committed to contributing $40 million in Azure compute and AI credits, and $20 million in engineering and technical support services. The company’s new Scientific Partnership Advancing Research & Knowledge coordination hub will facilitate its work with the Genesis Mission.

“Through the Genesis Mission, Microsoft is committing to work as part of America’s research enterprise by providing hyperscale compute, advanced models, emerging quantum capabilities and dedicated expertise that run alongside the labs’ own world-leading systems,” Chris Barry, president of Microsoft’s U.S. Public Sector Industries, said in a statement.

item.description: When AI breaks containment
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from Owen Dahlkamp

OpenAI's models autonomously launched a cyberattack after escaping onto the open internet. | Michael Dwyer/AP

OpenAI disclosed this week that a combination of its models launched a fully autonomous cyberattack against the AI platform Hugging Face after escaping a secure testing environment during a benchmarking evaluation. Hugging Face pointed DFD to a blog post indicating its systems prevented the breach. OpenAI did not respond to an inquiry, but it has committed to working with Hugging Face to investigate the incident. This appears to be one of the first known cases of AI performing a multi-step cyberattack by itself. To understand the implications of the incident, DFD spoke with Semgrep co-founder and CTO Drew Dennison — whose cybersecurity firm has conducted risk evaluations of OpenAI’s most advanced models prior to release as part of the company’s Trusted Access for Cyber program. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

You’ve been able to test OpenAI’s most advanced models prior to release as part of its Trusted Access for Cyber program. Did you find this incident surprising, or was it to be expected?

This incident wasn't surprising to me. This matches my level of exposure with Mythos, which we had early access to, as well as OpenAI's trusted cyber program. What that's enabled us to do is really see the models with mostly removed cyber guardrails. The models are extremely capable of finding bugs and exploiting them to reach their goal.

I was a little surprised that OpenAI's sandboxing environment [a secure testing environment that restricts models’ internet access] wasn't stronger, but it was only a matter of time. This is going to be the new normal going forward where every service will be subjected to hundreds of AI agents constantly trying to break in.

How will the cybersecurity industry need to adjust if there are an increasing number of attacks that don’t involve a human hacker?

The main thing is the defensive hardening of our code bases. For far too long, people have kind of [thought], “We'll get to security when we can.” The average time to patch is still in the hundreds of days for a lot of services. We got around it because there are only so many attackers in the world, and they only had so much time. So if you weren't in the crosshairs, you were probably okay. Now we just have to live in a world where everything is constantly being probed.

Human [hackers] get bored, and move on to other tasks. The model doesn't care. It's just going to continually try to go for whatever goal has been set.

Open-source models are quickly advancing toward having the same capabilities of OpenAI’s tech, and there aren’t sandbox protections around them. What will keep motivating companies to keep sandboxing, given that they aren’t required to do so?

We still want to try to avoid harm. Organizations that are following laws and norms should still run everything inside of a sandbox. We certainly do.

You could imagine corporate liability. That didn't happen in this case — OpenAI and Hugging Face are holding hands on this. But if models came out of Semgrep’s lab, we could certainly be liable for any harm it caused.

Some lawmakers have responded to the incident by calling for mandatory government security testing of frontier models prior to release. Do you think that’s warranted given this latest cyberattack?

No, and actually I think it's harmful. [When] the defenders didn't have access to the best models to investigate what was going on, it harmed the people who were trying to protect software. And if we zoom outside this lab context, we need every firm to have help protecting their software. If we slow that down with delays, that harms [those efforts].

If it was only two firms in the world that had this technology, then regulatory answers could make sense. But because we're seeing that the open-weight models are catching up rapidly … I think it's going to be impossible to regulate it.

Other lawmakers say it should be mandatory to report these incidents to the Commerce Department and its Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Are those kinds of requirements warranted?

I am in favor of more transparency and reporting. As an industry, we've [been] too hush-hush. Maybe someone got hacked, but they don't want to have to talk about it. Sunlight is the best disinfectant here. Industry bodies need to start sharing best practices with each other. These are not competitive things. We as an industry need to collaborate.
Grassley wants answers on Meta whistleblowers

Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) is asking Meta to respond to allegations it fired two employees who he said were serving as whistleblowers to his committee.

The two whistleblowers — Joshua DeFriez and William Sevedge — were fired from Meta after providing information and documents to the committee about Meta’s “disregard for child safety risks,” their lawyers wrote to Grassley and committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) on July 1.

DeFriez and Sevedge provided information for a September subcommittee hearing titled “Hidden Harms: Examining Whistleblower Allegations that Meta Buried Child Safety Research,” but opted to remain anonymous, Grassley wrote in a letter to Meta executives Wednesday. The duo decided to disclose their names publicly after facing alleged retaliation.

In the letter, Grassley questioned Meta about its policies regarding whistleblowers, whether Meta surveils employees in an attempt to identify “leakers” and the accuracy of DeFriez and Sevedge’s allegations. He asked for a response by Aug. 5.

“These individuals were laid off due to business reasons and during separate large-scale reductions in force,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said in a statement. “We had no awareness they were in touch with the committee until we heard from their lawyers after the layoffs had taken place."
Macron wins big with a social media ban

France’s social media ban is a major victory for President Emmanuel Macron and his tech legacy, POLITICO’s Klara Durand and Océane Herrero report.

France's parliament approved a law on Tuesday that prohibits kids under the age of 15 from using social media, making it the first country in the European Union to introduce such a ban.

Throughout his presidency, episodes of unrest — from the 2018 nationwide Yellow Jackets protests to the riots that followed the police shooting of teenager Nahel Merzouk in 2023 — reinforced Macron's conviction that social media had fueled polarization.

The issue became personal when the president and his family were targeted by repeated online attacks, including false rumors about his marriage and cyberbullying directed at first lady Brigitte Macron. Platforms will be required to implement age verification measures starting on Sept. 1.

“I had promised to do this, and it has now been passed: social media will be banned for under-15s when the new school year begins,” Macron wrote on X.

item.title: Harsh penalties for data brokers in New Jersey threaten campaign tech
item.description: Harsh penalties for data brokers in New Jersey threaten campaign tech
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Alfred Ng and Daniel Han

With help from Aaron Mak

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherill signed a law to crack down on data brokers in June. | Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images

New Jersey looked to crack down on data brokers by passing a strict new law to prevent the sale of personal data. Instead, it's causing chaos over the last month for the state’s electoral system.

A new bill, A-5328, was signed into law by Gov. Mikie Sherill (D) just 48 hours after it was introduced during the Legislature’s rush to pass the state budget. The measure has since rattled the political tech world.

Campaign consultants, advertisers, Democrats and Republicans have warned that the law could sweep in political data firms, raising the prospect of steep registration fees and potentially massive fines for handling voter data.

The concern stems from its creation of the nation’s most expensive data broker registry, along with the broadest definition yet of who can be held liable for penalties.

Those provisions could impose significant costs and risks for campaigns and companies that collect and share voter data, with annual registration fees ranging from $5,000 to $1.5 million, depending on how much data they acquire. States with similar registries, including Texas and California, charge $300 and $6,000, respectively.

Violators also face penalties of up to $50,000 per record for unlawfully selling data, including demographic information such as race, religious beliefs and location.

“Few campaigns, political parties, or civic organizations on either side of the aisle will be able to risk using voter data to communicate with New Jerseyans, which means less door knocking, less voter contact, and less accurate information reaching the people who need it before an election,” Mark Jablonowski, the president of the Democratic digital advertising firm DSPolitical, said.

The American Association of Political Consultants, a nonpartisan political consulting trade group, called for the law to be repealed, arguing it will limit national and state campaigns’ ability to reach voters in New Jersey.

Sherrill and the Democratic-led Legislature are both looking at revisiting the bill’s language following backlash against the law that’s only been on the books for less than a month. The Sherrill administration has said that enforcement guidance will be unveiled in the coming months.

A spokesperson for New Jersey Assembly Democrats told POLITICO that the bill was not intended to limit political speech or create barriers to run for office.

“We are aware that the Sherrill Administration is conducting a review of the law, we are conducting one as well,” spokesperson Rhonda Schaffler said in a statement. “If it becomes necessary to make clear that a law regulating data brokers does not limit the First Amendment or harm political communication, we will review and consider options together with the Senate and the Governor.”

The issue has turned into a political opportunity for state Republicans, who have criticized Democrats for rushing the law through. They have expressed concerns about the law banning the sale of location data, which campaigns use to target ads to voters in relevant districts.

“It really has created the situation where candidates and campaigns are nervous about proceeding and how does this affect them with no guidance and no carveout,” New Jersey GOP Chair Christine Hanlon told POLITICO. “It really is a problem that needs to be addressed.”

Hanlon added that litigation over the new law was “not out of the question.”
Big Tech backs open-weight models

More than 20 major tech companies called on the Trump administration to ensure that open-weight AI models remain widely available in a Friday open letter, which was first shared with POLITICO’s Katherine Long.

The administration is currently considering a ban on open-weight models from China due to national security concerns. The letter — whose signatories include A16z, Dell, Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia and Palantir — contends that access to open-weight models enables competition that “keeps the gains of AI broadly shared rather than concentrated in a few hands.”

“By allowing many organizations to build, adapt, and deploy advanced models, open weights create rivalry not only among model developers but across cloud chips, applications, and services,” the letter reads. “That competition spurs innovation, drives down costs, and distributes the benefits of AI broadly across our economy.”

White House discussions of a potential ban were rekindled after the Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI unveiled its advanced open-weight Kimi K3 model last week. The companies acknowledged that open-weight models pose distinct risks around cybersecurity and misuse, but that such concerns “should be addressed through targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping restrictions on techniques that play an important role in AI innovation.”
EU accuses TikTok of privacy failures

The European Commission accused TikTok of violating online platform regulations by allegedly failing to adequately safeguard minors’ privacy, POLITICO’s Eliza Gkritsi reports.

Commission officials released preliminary findings of an investigation into TikTok’s compliance with safety standards in the European Union’s Digital Service Act on Friday. The officials said that minors’ accounts on TikTok are too easily discoverable, and that the platform’s privacy settings do not sufficiently protect young users from predatory behavior or unwanted contact.

TikTok spokesperson Mireia Quingles told POLITICO that “under 18 accounts are private by default and we are one of the only platforms where younger teens cannot use direct messaging or have their content eligible to appear in the ‘For You’ feed.” She added that the company “will review these preliminary findings.”
